videos.title: 1.0 TCE engine problems in Renault and Dacia vehicles
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.0 TCE engine is the 3-cylinder turbocharged 
petrol unit used in Renault and Dacia vehicles.
It was first introduced in 2018 as the TCE 100 
H4Dt engine in the Clio and Capture. It was also
downgraded to TCE 90 later to fit into ecology 
rules. Then it was updated to the TCE 110 H5Dt
in 2020 and used in the Megane. Also, this engine 
was largely used in all Dacia models. And the same
engine was used in the Nissan Micra as the HR10DET 
with a different plastic cover and a Nissan logo,
but all technologies were the same.
When it comes to common problems,
I wouldn’t say these engines were as bad as they 
were originally expected to be. One of the common
issues is significant random punching in early 
model years between 2018 and 2020. But there was
a software update that fixed this issue. So if you 
experience a sudden loss of power, contact your
Renault dealership and have the update installed.
Also, these engines are prone to oil leaks,
especially there is a common leak in 
the valve cover seal. But fortunately,
it’s fixed with the new seal, and it’s a very 
cheap solution, so it's not a big problem here.
These engines use timing chains, and they are 
not eternal. Renault claims that the chain will
last the entire life of the engine, and they 
are not wrong, since when the chain fails,
the engine will die. But, on average, owners hear 
some minor rattling starting at 120,000 miles,
so it makes sense to replace the chain kit 
in these engines at 100,000 miles or 160,000
kilometers to avoid chain jumping or braking. 
It’s quite unpleasant that the phaser may also
require replacement at about 120,000 miles. So, 
if you consider driving your car for a long time,
you should replace the chain kit along with 
the phaser. Also, it’s important to use OEM
oil or at least choose something with 
the needed viscosity to avoid premature
failure of the phaser and chain tensioner. The 
difference between the 100 and 110-horsepower
engines is that the more powerful one has 
two phasers, while the 100-horsepower model
and 90-horsepower model has only an intake 
phaser, which makes it cheaper to service.
Also, the 100-horsepower model has no hydraulic 
lifters, while the more powerful version is
equipped with them. So, if you own the H4Dt model, 
you may need to adjust the valve clearance once
every 60-80 thousand miles. But the procedure 
is only needed when the engine runs roughly and
vibrates or loses power. If it works flawlessly, 
there is no need to invest in valve adjustment.
Also, one more significant difference between the 
two versions of the 1.0 TCE is the fuel injection
system. The 100-horsepower version has port 
injectors that are reliable and don’t usually
cause problems. The 110-horsepower engine has 
direct injection and suffers from intake valve
contamination. This is not a serious problem, but 
just a feature of all direct injection engines
that are used in city traffic and rarely 
run at high revolutions. Sooner or later,
the intake valves will get clogged, and this 
will affect the power and stability of the
engine's work. Fortunately, valve cleaning in 
a good garage is not an expensive service now.
Other than that, I don’t see a lot of problems 
with these engines. For their size and price,
they are quite good machines that have extremely 
low fuel consumption and are good for city driving
with good torque. You will feel a lack of power 
when trying to overtake someone on a highway,
but other than that, the engine 
doesn’t feel extremely underpowered.
Turbochargers sometimes have problems with 
wastegates getting stuck, and you feel a
loss of power and rough running, as well as 
get warnings and lights on the dashboard.
Fortunately, the engine has quite a simple 
turbocharger that is cheap and easy to repair.
I’ve seen some reports for excessive oil 
consumption, but I’m not sure if it’s very
common for these engines. They will certainly 
burn some oil, but as long as it’s less than
half a liter per 1000 miles, it should 
be fine and won’t cause any problems.
So, I don’t think the 1.0 TCE is a bad choice. The 
110-horsepower version seems to be a little more
modern in terms of technologies, but it also 
fails earlier since it powers larger vehicles
like the Megane, and gets a lot of wear and 
tear because of this. The TCE 90 and TCE 100
seem to be solid engines with affordable 
service costs, very good fuel economy,
and they don’t feel extremely underpowered. But, 
of course, like any modern engine, they need
extremely good maintenance to last long enough. 
And I believe 250,000 kilometers or 170,000 miles
is a good average lifespan that you should keep 
in mind if you own a car with such an engine.

hey everyone Brian your honest mechanic 
today we're tackling a crucial issue that
could be destroying your turbo engine without 
you even knowing it with over 20 years in the
business I've seen too many engines suffer from 
avoidable mistakes stick around to learn how to
protect your turbo and if you find this helpful 
please don't forget to press that like button
and subscribe all right let's get to the 
five things that damages turbo engines one
cold starts and immediate acceleration one of 
the most common mistakes I see and it's a big
one is the cold start Ando syndrome you know 
the drill it's a frosty morning you're running
late so you start your engine and immediately hit 
the gas sound familiar well I hate to break it to
you but this is one of the most damaging things 
you can do to your turbo engine why you ask when
you start a cold engine especially in freezing 
conditions the oil is as thick as molasses your
turbocharger which by the way can spin at speeds 
exceeding 200,000 revolutions per minute needs
proper lubrication ASAP accelerating hard before 
the oil has a chance to warm up that's a recipe
for disaster so what's the solution simple allow 
your engine to idle for 2 to 5 minutes before
driving it's just a few minutes of your time 
but it can add years to your engine's life two
lowquality fuel now let's talk about what you're 
putting in your tank the quality of fuel you use
it matters a lot turbochargers increase pressure 
in the combustion chamber which means your fuel
needs to withstand higher compression with without 
pre- igniting using lowquality or incorrect octane
fuel can lead to engine knocking or pre-ignition 
and trust me those little explosions in your
cylinders they're bad news for your engine always 
and I mean always refer to your vehicles owners's
manual for the recommended fuel grade if it says 
premium don't cheap out the few extra bucks at
the pump they're nothing compared to the cost of 
major engine repairs three overreliance on stop
start systems now let's talk talk about a feature 
in many modern turbocharged Vehicles stop start
systems they're great for fuel efficiency and 
Emissions but and it's a big butt they can be
trouble for turbo engines if you rely on them too 
heavily why it all comes down to oil circulation
every time the engine stops even for a few seconds 
oil flow ceases this can be a real problem if the
engine shuts off when the turbocharger is still 
hot over time this start Stop Cycle can lead to
increased wear oil cing and even damage to your 
starter motor and battery so what's the solution
use these systems wisely consider disabling 
the stop start system every once in a while
and always use highquality oil approved for 
stop start systems four immediate shutdown
after high-s speeed or high lad driving picture 
this scenario you've just finished a long Highway
Drive pull into your driveway and immediately 
shut off the engine sounds harmless right wrong
after high-speed or high load driving your 
turbocharger can reach temperatures over 1
1,000° F that's hotter than a pizza oven turning 
off the engine immediately cuts off the oil supply
leaving all that heat with nowhere to go the 
result oil cing where Oil essentially bakes
onto your turbochargers components not good the 
fix is simple let your engine idle for 30 seconds
to a minute after high stress driving before 
shutting it off it's a small step that can make
a big difference in your turbocharger lifespan 
five neglecting regular oil changes listen up
because this is crucial regular oil changes are 
the lifeblood of your turbo engine in a turbo
engine oil doesn't just lubricate it also helps 
cool the turbocharger and let me tell you that oil
degrades fast under those conditions skipping oil 
changes you might as well be throwing sand in your
engine so what should you do consider changing 
engine oil every 3,500 to 5,000 Mi and always use
high quality synthetic oil specifically formulated 
for turbocharged engines your turbo will thank you

smaller cars in the Renault Nissan
Alliance, including models like the DEA

Renault Captor, and even the Smart 44

primary goal was to offer good fuel
efficiency and lower emissions through
downsizing. While the turbocharger
compensated for the small displacement
by providing decent power for city and
suburban driving. Review and opinions.
Opinions on the 0.9 tce are somewhat
mixed, reflecting its downsized nature.
For urban driving, it's generally seen
as adequate. The turbo helps with
low-end torque, making it feel
reasonably spritly in traffic and at
lower speeds. On the open road/highway,
its limitations become more apparent. It
can feel strained at higher speeds and
overtaking maneuvers require careful
planning due to its modest power output.
Refinement. Being a threecylinder, it
has a characteristic thrum, especially
at idle and under acceleration. While
some find it charming, others might find
it less refined than four-cylinder
engines. Turbo lag is also a common
complaint, meaning there's a delay
before the power kicks in. Advantages:
Fuel efficiency claimed official figures
often show impressive fuel economy and
low CO2 emissions, contributing to lower
road tax in some regions. Compact and
lightweight, its small size and
lightweight benefit overall vehicle
dynamics and packaging. Good low-end
torque. The turbocharger provides a
useful boost of torque from low RPMs,
which is beneficial in city driving.
Indirect injection. Unlike many modern
turbocharged engines, the 0.9 tce uses
multi-point indirect fuel injection.
This is often cited as a major advantage
for long-term reliability as it avoids
carbon buildup on intake valves, a
common issue with direct injection
engines. Timing chain uses a timing
chain which is generally
maintenance-free for the life of the
engine unlike timing belts that require
periodic replacement. Disadvantages
limited power at higher speeds. The
small displacement means it can struggle
to maintain speed on inclines or during
rapid acceleration at highway speeds.
Noticeable threecylinder
thrum/vibrations.
While balanced, it still has the
inherent characteristic vibrations of a
three-cylinder engine. Turbo lag. There
could be a noticeable delay between
pressing the accelerator and the turbo
spooling up, leading to a slight
hesitation. Less refined for
enthusiastic driving. It's not an engine
for those seeking a sporty driving
experience. Potential for high realworld
fuel consumption. While official figures
are low, aggressive driving or frequent
highway use can significantly increase
actual fuel consumption as the turbo is
constantly working harder. Common faults
and breakdowns. The 0.9 tce is generally
considered more reliable than the
problematic 1.2TC
H5. It overlaps with largely due to its
indirect injection system. However, it's
not without its issues. Thermostat
housing leaks. This is one of the more
frequently reported issues. The plastic
thermostat housing can become brittle
and crack leading to coolant leaks. Oil
and intake manifold/PCV
valve issues. Some owners have reported
oil residue in the intake manifold which
can sometimes be linked to a stuck or
faulty crankase ventilation PCV valve.
While not as severe as the oil burning
in the 1.2TCE,
it's worth monitoring. Low compression
on cylinders. Rare but severe. There are
isolated but concerning reports of low
compression in individual cylinders,
especially cylinder 2, often at
relatively low mileage, eg 36k m. This
can be a sign of internal engine damage
requiring significant repair or engine
replacement. The exact cause isn't
always clear without stripping the
engine, but it highlights a potential
serious mechanical vulnerability.
Ignition coil/spark plug issues. Like
many modern engines, faults with
ignition coils or spark plugs can lead
to misfires and rough running.
Turbocharger issues. While generally
durable for a small turbo, isolated
failures can occur. As with any forced
induction engine, these often present as
a loss of power or unusual noises. Fuel
consumption. Official combined fuel
consumption figures for the 0.9 TCE90HP
often range from 4.3 to 4.7L/100KM.
Real world consumption varies widely
based on driving style and conditions.
Owners on forums report figures from 5.0
to 6.5 L/100km
for mixed driving with careful drivers
sometimes achieving lower. It can reach
7.0 0 to 8.0 L/100 km in heavy city
traffic or with very aggressive driving
on a highway as the small engine has to
work harder. Timing. The Renault 0.9 tce
H4BT engine uses a timing chain. This is
a positive point for long-term ownership
as timing chains are designed to last
the life of the engine and do not
require regular replacement like timing
belts. However, issues with chain
stretch or tensioners can still occur,
though less frequently than in some
other engines. Autodoc even suggests a
recommended part replacement interval of
every 150,000 km for the timing chain,
implying it's not strictly for life in
all cases. Oil oil type. Renault
typically specifies engine oils
conforming to Renault RN07000
or Renault RN0710
standards for the 0.9 tce. Common
viscosities include 5W, 30 or 5W 40,
adhering to ACIA A3/B4
or ACIA C3 specifications. Always check
your vehicle's owner's manual for the
precise recommended oil type and
specification for your specific model
and year. Oil capacity. The oil capacity
for the 0.9 tce H4BT is typically around
4.2 to 4.3 L. Importance. Using the
correct specification and highquality
oil is crucial for the longevity of this
small turbocharged engine, especially
for the turbocharger and timing chain.
Given the engine's compact nature,
regular oil changes at recommended
intervals or even slightly more
frequently for heavy urban use are
highly advisable. Versions and history.
Initial release. The 0.9 tce
debuted around 2012, notably in the
Renault Cleo 4. Power output. Most
common version is the TC90 90HP/66
kW. There was also a TCE75,
75HP/56KW
and a higher output TCE 110, 109HP/80KW
found in sportier versions like the
Twingo GT. application found in a wide
range of compact cars and small SUVs
across the Renault Nissan Mitsubishi
Alliance including Renault Cleo 4,
Captor Eye, Twingo 3, Dea Sander 2,
Logan 2, Docker, Logi, Early Duster Eye,
Smart for 4, Smart42 as part of the
Daimler collaboration. It has largely
been superseded by the newer 1.0TCE, 0
tce, H4DT/H5DT,
and 1.3TC,
H5H engines in more recent models. In
summary, the Renault 0.9TCE
H4BT engine is a good choice for urban
and suburban driving, offering decent
efficiency and enough power for its
intended purpose. Its indirect injection
system is a notable reliability
advantage over some direct injection
counterparts. However, its small size
means it can feel strained on highways
and potential buyers should be aware of
known issues like thermostat housing
leaks and rare but serious low
compression problems. Regular and
diligent maintenance, especially with
the correct engine oil, is key to its
long-term reliability. Thank you for
watching the video and I invite you to

Greetings to everyone and see you in the
next episode. See you soon.

rail injection turbocharged diesel
engine that has been in production since
2001. its longevity and widespread
adoption across numerous brands in the

incorporating features like common rail
injection, variable geometry
turbochargers, VGT on higher output

reduction STR in later iterations, often

85 kW, or even 120hp, 88 kW in later,
more powerful versions. Widespread
application found in a vast array of
vehicles. Renault, Cleo, Meane, Scenic,

the earlier flaws. Overall, when

its excellent fuel economy, decent
torque for its size, and relatively
smooth operation for small diesel.
Advantages: Exceptional fuel economy.
This is arguably the K9K's biggest
strength. It's renowned for delivering
very low fuel consumption figures,
especially on long runs. Strong low-end
torque. The turbocharger provides good
pulling power from low RPMs, making it
feel responsive in city traffic and
capable of highway cruising. Widespread
availability of parts and expertise due
to its vast production numbers. Parts
are readily available and many mechanics
are familiar with the engine.
Refinement. Later versions. Newer
versions with improved common rail
systems and better sound deadening are
quite refined for a small diesel.
Disadvantages. Vulnerability of early
versions. The wellocumented issues of
early K9K engines significantly tarnish
its overall reputation. Diesel specific
maintenance requires attention to DPF
regeneration on equipped models. AdBlue

vehicles might feel less lively.
Complexity. Modern common rail diesel

repairs, when needed, can be expensive.
Common faults and breakdowns. This is
where the history of the 1.5DCI
becomes critical. The engine's
reputation was heavily impacted by
widespread issues in its earlier
versions, roughly up to 4 per early 5
standards before major revisions in the
late 2000s, early 2010s. Main bearing
failure, crankshaft bearings. This was
the most notorious and catastrophic
fault. A design flaw often linked to oil
starvation due to manufacturing
tolerances or poor oil
circulation/quality
led to premature wear and failure of the
crankshaft connecting rod bearings. This
typically resulted in a loud knocking
noise followed by complete engine
seizure. This issue was particularly
prevalent in early high output versions,
eG 100/105hp.
Injector problems. Faulty or leaking
injectors, particularly with early Deli
fuel injection systems were common. This
could lead to misfires, rough running,
excessive smoke, and poor fuel economy.
High-pressure fuel pump, HBFP, failure,
also linked to earlier deli systems. If
the HBFB failed, it could shed metal
fragments into the fuel system,
contaminating injectors and the fuel
rail, leading to very costly repairs.
Turbocharger failure. While not unique
to the 1.5DCI,
turbocharger failures were relatively
common, sometimes exacerbated by the
main bearing issues, lack of oil
pressure or neglected oil changes. Later
versions, generally Euro5 and Euro6 post
2010, especially after 2015 revisions
with blue DCI have significantly
improved reliability. While no engine is
immune to issues, the systemic design
flaws leading to catastrophic failures
were largely addressed. Modern K9K
engines are generally considered
reliable with issues more commonly being
DPF clogging common to all modern
diesels, especially with frequent short
trips that don't allow for proper
regeneration cycles. EGR valve issues
can get clogged with soot leading to
performance issues and warning lights.

chain. This is a critical maintenance

recommended replacement interval
typically varies by year and model, but
generally falls between 120,000 km to
160,000 km or every 5 to 6 years,
whichever comes first. Consequences of
neglect. Failure to replace the timing

to catastrophic engine damage, bent

typically ACIA A3/B4

specification and maintaining strict oil
change intervals are absolutely critical
for the longevity of the 1.5 DCI,
especially for protecting the
turbocharger and in older versions,
mitigating bearing wear. Many experts
recommend shortening manufacturer oil
change intervals, eg from 30,000 km to
15,000 to 20,000 km or annually to
enhance engine life, particularly for
older K9K engines or those doing short
urban trips. In summary, the Renault
1.5DCI
K9K is a ubiquitous diesel engine with a
long and somewhat checkered history.
Early versions suffered from severe and
well doumented reliability issues,
particularly regarding main bearings and
fuel injection components. However,
later generations, especially those from
around 2010 onwards, have seen
significant improvements in reliability,
becoming a much more robust and
dependable engine. For prospective
buyers of used cars with this engine, a
thorough service history is paramount.
Specifically looking for evidence of
regular and correct oil changes and
timing belt replacements. Given its
excellent fuel economy, the 1.5DCI could
be a great choice for those who do

engine specific version and maintenance
is essential. Thank you for watching the

videos.title: Qashqai 1.2 DIG-T engine problems (1.2 Turbo)
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.2 DIG-T engine in the Qashqai and Juke 
models is the same engine as the H5Ft or
1.2 TCe in Renault and Dacia vehicles. It was 
manufactured between 2012 and 2019. The first
years were prone to a lot of software-related 
problems and could just stall or lose power
randomly, so Renault-Nissan issued several 
software updates that surprisingly fixed the
issues. If you experience random unexplained 
problems with the early-model-year 1.2 DIG-T,
make sure you have the latest available 
software update installed in the dealership.
These engines are very economical. And even 
though the horsepower is not mind-blowing at all,
the torque is very decent, and driving the 
Qashqai powered with this engine is a lot of
fun in the city traffic. For highways, you would 
want more power, but still, it’s not that bad.
Also, this is a 4-cylinder engine, 
so there are no vibrations and
juddering that you will get in 3-cylinder 
engines of such size in many other cars.
Among the common problems, I would point out 
oil consumption. The engine will start burning
some oil from the first miles of its life, and it 
will deteriorate gradually. The reason is simple:
the piston rings are not perfect and let 
some oil leak into the combustion chamber.
Repair is super expensive, so the obvious solution 
is to put up with this and just keep an eye on
the oil level to avoid low-pressure issues.
Secondly, these engines have direct injection,
and this inevitably leads to carbon buildup on 
intake valves sooner or later. If you experience
hesitation, uneven idle, or even stalling, this 
is clearly because of the contaminated valves that
need to be cleaned. Fortunately, cleaning is not 
that expensive in a good independent repair shop.
These engines are equipped with the timing chain 
and it’s not perfect. The chain is quite thin and
will elongate significantly up to 60,000 miles, 
or 100,000 kilometers. The chain kit is not that
expensive and the labor cost may not be that 
bad. But the problem is that both camshafts
are equipped with phasers for variable valve 
timing and these phasers are very often dead
at this mileage, so it makes sense to replace 
them when you are installing the new chain. The
phasers are not cheap at all and this makes the 
chain kit replacement ridiculously expensive.
And there is one more very common problem: the 
seal of the crankcase ventilation system pipe is
somehow very unreliable and may get a crack at any 
mileage. It’s not hard or expensive to replace,
but it’s very hard to locate this problem. 
So, if you experience oil pressure anomalies,
random check engine light, or unstable 
engine work, it’s a good idea to check
this seal in the PCV system first.
Other than that, these engines are
quite good to own. They will survive about 
150,000 miles or 240,000 kilometers without
major problems. But after that oil consumption is 
usually too high and extremely expensive repairs
are needed which usually means engine replacement. 
So, it’s important to know all the weaknesses when
you own a high-mileage Qashqai or are about to 
buy a used vehicle equipped with this engine.

videos.title: What Causes a Diesel Engine to Lose Power? (5 COMMON Causes)
videos.transcript_text:
If your diesel is losing power, there
are a few things you can check before
heading to the mechanic and spending
thousands. In this video, I am going to
show you the five most common causes of
diesel power loss that you can actually
diagnose yourself. Make sure to watch
till the end because I'll give you the
exact order to check these issues,
starting with the cheapest fixes first.
Let's get started. Number one, clogged
fuel filter. The most common reason your
diesel is losing power is a clogged fuel
filter. This happens to almost every
diesel owner at some point and it's
responsible for more power loss
complaints than any other single issue.
Your fuel filter protects your engine
from dirt, water, and debris in the
fuel. But over time, it gets packed with
contaminants and can't flow fuel
properly. Most diesel engines have two
filters, primary and secondary. And when
either gets clogged, your engine starts
starving for fuel. The symptoms are
obvious power loss during acceleration,
especially when going uphill or
overtaking. Your engine might sputter or
hesitate under load. You'll notice it
most when your engine needs fuel the
most. The fix is simple. Replace both
filters at the same time. Don't just do
one because if one is clogged, the other
isn't far behind. Number two, bad glow
plugs. Glow plugs heat up your
combustion chambers to help diesel
ignite properly. When they fail, your
engine struggles to start and runs
poorly, especially when cold. Unlike
spark plugs in gas engines, glow plugs
don't fire continuously, but they're
critical for proper combustion. When
they go bad, you'll notice hard
starting, especially in cold weather,
white smoke from the exhaust, and
reduced power until the engine warms up.
Bad glow plugs cause incomplete
combustion, which means less power and
more carbon buildup throughout your
engine. You might also notice rough
idling and engine misfiring. Number
three, dirty fuel injectors. Diesel fuel
injectors spray fuel at over 23,000 PSI
with precision timing. When they get
dirty or clogged, they can't deliver the
right amount of fuel to each cylinder,
and your power drops immediately. This
is especially common if you've been
using lower quality diesel fuel or
haven't changed your fuel filters
regularly. The injectors get gked up
with carbon deposits and can't atomize
the fuel properly. You'll notice rough
idling, black smoke from the exhaust,
engine misfiring, and that frustrating
loss of power. Your fuel economy will
also tank because the engine is working
harder but getting less done. You can
try out a good quality fuel injector
cleaner and see if things improve. If
not, then you need to go for
professional cleaning or replacement.
Number four, clogged BPF filter. The
diesel particulate filter captures soot
from your exhaust to reduce emissions.
But when it gets clogged, it's like
putting a cork in your exhaust pipe, and
your engine can't breathe out. This is
especially common if you do a lot of
short trips or city driving. The DPF
needs highway speeds and sustained heat
to burn off the accumulated soot.
Without that, it just keeps filling up
until it's blocked. You'll see a DPF
warning light on your dashboard,
experience reduced power, and your
engine might go into limp mode. Fuel
consumption will increase because the
engine is working harder to push exhaust
through the clogged filter. The solution
is often a good highway drive at
sustained speeds to trigger
regeneration, but severely clogged
filters need professional cleaning.
Number five, dirty air filter. Your
engine needs massive amounts of air to
burn fuel efficiently. A dirty air
filter restricts this air flow and can
cause surprisingly significant power
loss. This is one of the easiest
problems to diagnose and fix. Pop the
hood, locate your air filter housing,
and check if the filter looks dirty or
clogged. If it's gray or black instead
of white or light colored, it's choking
your engine. A dirty air filter causes
gradual power loss, poor acceleration,
and can even trigger black smoke because
the fuel to air ratio gets thrown off.
Your engine is essentially suffocating.
The fix costs about $20 and takes 5
minutes. Just replace the filter with a
quality replacement. Most of these
problems are preventable with basic
maintenance. Change your oil every 5,000
mi with highquality diesel oil. This is
crucial for keeping your turbocharger
and other components properly
lubricated. Change your fuel filters
every 10,000 to 15,000 mi. Replace your
air filter when it's dirty. and test
your glow plugs regularly, especially
before winter. Use a quality fuel
injector cleaner every 6,000 miles to
keep your injectors clean and prevent
carbon buildup. This simple step can
save you thousands in injector
replacement cost down the road. Use
quality diesel fuel from reputable
stations and don't ignore warning
lights. For DPF issues, take your truck
on the highway regularly to keep it
clean. If you're experiencing power
loss, start with the cheapest fixes
first. Check your air filter, then your
fuel filters before moving on to glow
plugs and injectors.

significant problems. Excessive oil

ignored oil consumption. Engines could

turbocharging. However, real world fuel

7LKM
on highways to 10 to 11LKM

suggest that if the engine is burning
oil, fuel efficiency can also be
negatively impacted. Timing. The Renault

H5F engines use a timing chain. This
component is theoretically designed to
last the life of the engine. However, as
mentioned under disadvantages, premature
timing chain stretch and tensioner
failure are known problems with this
engine, often necessitating costly
replacement. This issue is sometimes
linked to oil quality and change
intervals. Oil oil type. Renault
generally recommended oils conforming to
their RN07000
or RN0710
specifications often with ACIA A3/B4
or ACIS C3 and viscosities like 5W30
or 5W40. Crucial recommendation for this
engine due to the known oil consumption
issues is highly recommended to check
oil levels very frequently, far more
often than typical recommendations,
possibly every 1,000 to 2,000 km. Use
high quality synthetic oil, adhering
strictly to manufacturer specifications,
or even using a slightly more robust
oil, eg higher HDHS viscosity if
recommended for the climate. Reduce oil
change intervals. Many specialists and
affected owners advise changing the oil
much more frequently than the
manufacturers suggested 20,000 km or
30,000 km, often recommending every
10,000 km or annually. Consider engine
flush treatments before oil changes to
help remove sludge and carbon deposits.
In summary, the Renault 1.2TCE 2TCE H5F
engine, while offering decent
performance and refinement when new, has
a documented history of significant
reliability issues, primarily related to
excessive oil consumption, timing chain
problems, and carbon buildup, which can
lead to costly repairs, or even engine
replacement. Prospective buyers of used
vehicles with this engine should
exercise extreme caution. Ensure a full
service history is available and ideally
have a thorough pre-purchase inspection
that specifically checks for these known
problems. Regular and diligent oil
checks and more frequent oil changes
than factory recommendations are
critical for owners of these engines.
The newer 1.2TCE 2TCE HR12 3-cylinder
engine is a different design and does
not carry the same problematic
reputation as the older H5F. Thank you
for watching the video and I invite you
to subscribe to the Automotoreak
channel. Greetings to everyone and see
you in the next episode. See you soon.

videos.title: Never BUY this Peugeot ENGINE | Puretech Peugeot
videos.transcript_text:
pu's pure Tech Engine promised to be a
revolution in the efficiency and
performance of gasoline engines with its
compact design low fuel consumption and
Innovative technology this engine
conquered the market and received
several Awards but over time what seemed
to be a resounding success became a
problem for thousands of owners today we
tell you the whole story from its
characteristics to the great controversy
that forced PUO to take urgent
measures to understand why the pure Tech
has been so much talked about let's
first look at its main features it is a
family of three cylinder gasoline
engines with displacements of 1.0 and
1.2 L developed by the PSA group today's
stantis with the aim of offering
efficiency without sacrificing power one
of the key points of its design is the
reduction of internal friction and the
use of an oil immersed timing belt
instead of a traditional metal chain
this decision was intended to reduce
noise and improve lubrication optimizing
engine performance and extending engine
life thanks to these Innovations pure
Tech engines achieved reduced fuel
consumption lower emissions and
surprising performance for their size
with turbocharged versions reaching up
to 130 horsepower however what began as
an advantage soon became a headache for
owners beginning in 2020 numerous
reports of serious failures began to to
emerge the problem was in its timing
belt in many cases the timing belt was
degrading prematurely coming apart
inside the engine and causing internal
damage the most common symptoms were
increased oil consumption loss of power
and lubrication system failure in the
worst cases the deteriorated belt
clogged the oil ducts causing
catastrophic failures that rendered the
engines unusable pujo and stellantis
tried to minimize the problem at first
but the number of vehicles affected made
it impossible to ignore it is estimated
that hundreds of thousands of units in
Europe were impacted by this def
prompting the company to launch an
action plan in March 2024 stellantis
announced an extended warranty for the
affected engines covering repair costs
for up to 10 years or
175,000 km in addition they offered
refunds to those owners who had already
paid for repairs provided they had been
serviced at official dealers
but the real solution came with a third
generation of pure Tech engines launched
in 2023 which replaced the controversial
oil bathed belt with a timing chain
eliminating the root of the problem that
affected thousands of customers and for
you how bad is this engine leave your
opinion below
[Music]

Your diesel engine is built tough, but
certain habits can send it to an early
grave. Today, I am exposing six deadly
mistakes that are silently killing your
diesel engine and how to avoid them.
Without wasting any more time, let's get
started. One, running too many short
trips. Cold diesel engines suffer
dramatically more wear than properly
warmed up ones. Those quick grocery runs
and school drop offs never allow your
engine to reach optimal temperature.
Your particulate filter can't
regenerate. Unburnt fuel dilutes your
oil and moisture accumulates throughout
the system. If short trips are
unavoidable, take your diesel for a
30inut highway run weekly to clear the
system. Two, lugging the engine in high
gears. That massive low-end torque is
tempting, but constantly lugging your
diesel at extremely low RPMs damages
both engine and transmission. Despite
what many believe, running at the
absolute lowest RPM isn't efficient.
It's
destructive. Diesel engines have a
specific power band that must be
respected. Downshift when needed and let
the engine work within its design
parameters. Three, changing engine oil
late. Diesel fuel may lubricate, but
engine oil is your engine's lifeblood.
When manufacturers recommend oil changes
every 12,000 mi, experienced diesel
owners know better. Frequent oil changes
are the single most effective way to
extend your diesel's life. I recommend
that you change your oil every 5,000 mi.
High mileage drivers often cut those
intervals in half for a reason.
Contaminated oil becomes abrasive,
accelerating internal wear with every
mile. Four, excessive idling.
Many diesel owners leave their engines
idling for extended periods, thinking
it's easier on the starter. In reality,
idling causes excessive moisture buildup
in the exhaust and oil, prevents proper
DPF regeneration, and accelerates carbon
deposits. Unless you're in extreme cold,
modern diesels don't benefit from long
warm-ups. They need to work under proper
load. Five, using lowquality fuel.
Diesel injection systems operate under
extreme pressure up to 30,000 PSI in
modern engines. Poor quality fuel
introduces contaminants that score
precision components while water in fuel
promotes internal corrosion. The first
sign of fuel system issues is usually
declining MPG followed by increased soot
production. By then, expensive damage
has already begun. Six, ignoring DPF
regeneration cycles. Modern diesel
engines need to regularly regenerate
their particulate filters at
temperatures around 600° C or
1,112° F. This process takes 15 to 20
minutes of specific driving conditions.
Many owners interrupt these cycles by
turning off their engines prematurely or
never driving long enough to initiate
regeneration. If you notice signs of
regeneration starting, slight change in
engine note, increased idle speed,
cooling fans running, complete your
journey rather than shutting down.
Consistently interrupted regeneration
cycles will eventually lead to expensive
DPF replacement and potential engine
damage. Number seven, babying your
diesel engine.
Believe it or not, always driving your
diesel gently can actually harm it.
Diesel engines need occasional higher
RPM driving to clear carbon deposits and
ensure complete combustion. Always
staying under 2500 RPM and never using
full throttle leads to carbon buildup,
clogged EGR valves, and sluggish
turbochargers. The solution? Once
weekly, find a safe stretch of highway
and run your engine through its full RPM
range for a few minutes. This Italian
tuneup clears deposits, exercises the
turbo, and helps maintain proper
cylinder pressures, extending your
engine's life without any costly
repairs. Remember, diesel engines are
incredibly durable when treated
properly.
By avoiding these seven destructive
habits, your diesel can easily surpass
300,000 mi of reliable service.
Like this video and subscribe for more
practical automotive advice that saves
you money and extends your engine's

Did you know that diesel engines
operating primarily at low loads and
city speeds can lose up to 40% of their
efficiency over time due to carbon
buildup? There's one simple technique
that experienced mechanics have been
using in secret for decades to reverse
this damage and extend engine life by
hundreds of thousands of miles. Today,
I'm revealing a technique so simple that
most diesel owners dismiss it as too
easy to work. But this method has kept
most diesel vehicles running strong for
over 400,000 mi. while some face
expensive repairs and early engine
replacements. Make sure to watch till
the end because I'll reveal the exact
procedure and timing that makes this
technique work, plus the warning signs
that tell you when your diesel
desperately needs this treatment. Let's
start with why your diesel engine is
slowly choking itself to death. The
problem with modern diesel driving
patterns. Modern diesel vehicles are
incredible machines designed to last
hundreds of thousands of miles. But
there's one thing they weren't designed
for. The way most people actually drive
them. Diesel engines were originally
developed for constant work at varying
loads. Think farm tractors, long haul
trucks, and marine applications where
the engine regularly operates across its
entire RPM range under different load
conditions. But today's diesel owners
use their vehicles primarily for
commuting, school runs, grocery
shopping, and city driving. These short
trips at low speeds create the perfect
conditions for carbon buildup throughout
your engine systems. Here's what happens
during typical modern diesel driving.
Your engine rarely reaches full
operating temperature. It operates
primarily at low RPMs with light loads.
The exhaust system never gets hot enough
to burn off carbon deposits. Your DPF
system struggles to complete
regeneration cycles. Over time, this
driving pattern creates a cascade of
problems. Carbon deposits build up in
your intake system, reducing air flow.
Your EGR system becomes clogged with
soot and carbon. Your DPF fills with
particles faster than it can burn them
off. Your turbocharger develops carbon
buildup that affects performance. The
result is an engine that gradually loses
power, efficiency, and reliability, even
though nothing is technically broken.
This is where the Italian tuneup becomes
essential. What exactly is an Italian
tuneup? The Italian tuneup isn't a real
tuneup at all. It's a driving technique
that involves running your diesel engine
at higher RPMs and loads for an extended
period to burn off carbon deposits and
restore proper operation. The technique
gets its name from the stereotype that
Italian drivers are aggressive, but the
science behind it is solid. High engine
loads and RPMs create the heat and air
flow necessary to clean carbon deposits
naturally. For diesel vehicles, the
Italian tuneup serves multiple critical
functions. It completes DPF regeneration
cycles that may have been interrupted
during city driving. It burns carbon
deposits off intake valves and EGR
components. It exercises your
turbocharger across its full operating
range. It brings all engine systems up
to proper operating temperatures. The
key is doing this safely and
systematically, not just driving
aggressively without purpose. How to
perform the Italian tuneup on your
diesel vehicle. The proper Italian
tuneup for diesel vehicles requires
specific conditions and procedures to be
effective and safe. First, ensure your
vehicle is in good mechanical condition.
Check your oil level and condition.
Verify the coolant levels are adequate
and make sure your air filter isn't
severely clogged. Don't attempt this
procedure if you have any warning lights
or known mechanical issues. Choose the
right driving conditions. You need a
highway or rural road where you can
maintain higher speeds safely for 15 to
20 minutes. This isn't something you can
do in city traffic or residential areas.
Here's the step-by-step procedure. Start
with a normal warm-up period. Drive
normally for the first 5 to 10 minutes
to bring your engine up to operating
temperature. Don't begin the high load
driving until your engine is fully
warmed up. Once warmed up, accelerate
firmly but smoothly to highway speeds.
You want to reach 2,500 to 3,500
revolutions per minute in the highest
gear you can maintain safely. For most
diesel vehicles, this means 65 to 75 mph
on level highway. Maintain this speed
and load for 15 to 20 minutes. You're
not trying to set speed records or drive
dangerously. You're simply keeping your
engine in its upper operating range long
enough for the heat and air flow to do
their work. During this period, your
diesel will try to clear carbon buildup.
After the high load period, return to
normal driving. Don't immediately shut
off the engine after hard driving. Allow
a few minutes of normal operation for
temperatures to stabilize. Why this
technique works for diesel engines? The
Italian tuneup is particularly effective
for diesel engines because of how diesel
combustion works and the operating
characteristics of modern diesel
vehicles. Diesel engines rely on high
compression and temperature for
efficient combustion. When operating at
low loads for extended periods,
combustion temperatures remain
relatively low, allowing carbon deposits
to form and accumulate. Highload
operation raises combustion temperature
significantly hot enough to burn off
these carbon deposits. The increased air
flow also helps carry away loosened
deposits through the exhaust system. For
turbocharged diesels, which includes
most modern vehicles, the Italian tuneup
exercises the turbocharger across its
full operating range. This helps prevent
carbon buildup on the turbine and
compressor wheels and keeps the variable
geometry mechanisms operating freely.
The technique is especially beneficial
for diesel particulate filter systems.
Extended high temperature operation
allows the DPF to complete full
regeneration cycles, burning off
accumulated soot that may not have been
eliminated during normal driving. EGR
systems also benefit from the increased
exhaust temperatures and flow rates,
which help burn off carbon deposits that
can cause valve sticking and flow
restrictions. When to perform the
Italian tuneup? For most diesel vehicle
owners, performing the Italian tuneup
every 2 weeks provides the right balance
of effectiveness and practicality.
However, your specific driving patterns
may require adjustments to the schedule.
If you do primarily highway driving with
regular longer trips, you may be
naturally performing the equivalent of
an Italian tuneup during normal
operation. In this case, a monthly
schedule might be sufficient. If you
drive primarily in city traffic with
short trips, you may need to perform the
procedure weekly to prevent carbon
buildup from becoming problematic. Pay
attention to warning signs that indicate
your diesel needs this treatment
immediately. reduced power or
acceleration, black smoke during
acceleration, rough idling or engine
vibration, decreased fuel economy, DPF
warning lights, or frequent regeneration
cycles. If you notice any of these
symptoms, perform the Italian tuneup as
soon as safely possible. Don't wait for
your regular schedule if your engine is
showing signs of carbon buildup. Regular
Italian tuneups can dramatically extend
the life and improve the performance of
diesel vehicles used primarily for city
driving or short trips. Fleet operators
who implement regular high load
operation report significantly longer
DPF life, reduced EGR system problems,
and better overall engine longevity.
Many achieve over 400,000 mi with
minimal emission system problems by
incorporating this technique into their
maintenance routines. Individual owners
report restored power and fuel economy,
especially in vehicles that had
gradually lost performance over time.
The technique can often restore 10 to
15% of lost power in vehicles with
significant carbon buildup. The
procedure also helps prevent expensive
emission system repairs. DPF
replacements can cost $3,000 to $6,000,
while EGR system cleaning or replacement
can run $1,500 to $3,000. Regular
Italian tune-ups can help prevent these
failures by maintaining system
cleanliness. Perhaps most importantly,
the technique helps diesel vehicles
operate as designed. Modern diesels are
sophisticated machines that perform best
when all systems function properly. The
Italian tuneup helps maintain this
proper operation despite driving
patterns that don't naturally provide
the conditions diesel engines need.
Alternative methods for diesel owners
who can't perform highway driving. Not
every diesel owner has access to
highways or conditions suitable for
traditional Italian tuneups. There are
alternative approaches that can provide
similar benefits like using quality and
proven additives. Remember, this isn't
about driving aggressively or
dangerously. It's about giving your
diesel engine the operating conditions
it needs to maintain proper function and
longevity. And that's it for today. If
you find this video helpful, please
don't forget to like and share. Thanks
for watching. And if you made it this
far, I really appreciate

videos.title: Renault 1.3 TCe engine: Common problems and faults
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.3 TCe engine was developed in 2017-2018, 
and it wasn’t just the Renault engine. It was
engineered by Renault-Nissan and Mercedes, 
and it has been used in a bunch of Mercedes,
Nissan, Renault, and Dacia vehicles. Actually, 
it’s a very reliable engine compared to other
downsized motors available on the market. And 
owners usually write good reviews about it.
In this video, I will focus on the problems 
and faults that you may experience with
this engine in Renault cars, but I should 
say that this is one of the best gasoline
engines made by Renault within the last decade.
First of all, it’s the 4-cylinder engine with a
good and reliable Garrett turbocharger. 
It has a very reliable timing chain,
which is quite unusual for modern engines. 
The chain can last about 250,000 kilometers,
and then it should be replaced along with 
the phasers, which is not that cheap,
but still, the lifespan is impressive. 
Also, the engine has hydraulic lifters,
so no need to adjust the valves.
The engine has direct injection,
which means the petrol is injected into 
the cylinders, and the intake valves
gradually get carbon buildup, especially if 
you mainly drive in city traffic. This means
that once every 30-40 thousand kilometers, the 
engine will require valve cleaning. Otherwise,
it will gradually lose power, and the 
revolutions will start jumping when idling.
Pay attention that the spark plugs will have to 
be replaced once every 30,000 kilometers. Somehow,
the plugs and coils don’t last long in 
these engines, probably because of a lot
of heat in their area. Also, if you feel 
sudden power loss, pay attention to the
turbocharger piping. It’s a very common issue 
when one of the pipes falls off and the engine
goes crazy. Fortunately, it's a quick DIY 
repair to put the pipe back in its place.
The engine will start consuming oil after about 
150,000 kilometers, and the consumption will
grow step by step. Unless it’s more than 1 
liter per 1000 kilometers, there is nothing
to worry about. But the engine has quite 
limited possibilities for repairs since it
doesn’t have iron sleeves in the block. Instead, 
it uses cylinder coating for better efficiency,
but once something is wrong with the block, the 
engine is dead. So, very high oil consumption
will tell you about the need to replace the 
engine unless there is a leak that you can find.
I wouldn’t say the engine is very cool to drive, 
especially if you love active driving. It has
a significant turbo lag and is not tuned 
for sporty driving at all. Additionally,
you shouldn’t expect magically good 
fuel consumption. It burns surprisingly
much fuel unless you barely touch the gas pedal.
Other than that, these are quite good engines that
can last up to 300 or even 350 thousand kilometers 
if maintained well. But they require high-quality
oil, and also expensive chain kit replacement, 
as well as periodic intake valve cleaning.

sudden power loss, pay attention to the

turbocharger piping. It’s a very common issue 
when one of the pipes falls off and the engine

goes crazy. Fortunately, it's a quick DIY 
repair to put the pipe back in its place.

The engine will start consuming oil after about 
150,000 kilometers, and the consumption will

grow step by step. Unless it’s more than 1 
liter per 1000 kilometers, there is nothing

to worry about. But the engine has quite 
limited possibilities for repairs since it

doesn’t have iron sleeves in the block. Instead, 
it uses cylinder coating for better efficiency,

but once something is wrong with the block, the 
engine is dead. So, very high oil consumption

will tell you about the need to replace the 
engine unless there is a leak that you can find.

I wouldn’t say the engine is very cool to drive, 
especially if you love active driving. It has

a significant turbo lag and is not tuned 
for sporty driving at all. Additionally,

you shouldn’t expect magically good 
fuel consumption. It burns surprisingly

much fuel unless you barely touch the gas pedal.
Other than that, these are quite good engines that

can last up to 300 or even 350 thousand kilometers 
if maintained well. But they require high-quality

oil, and also expensive chain kit replacement, 
as well as periodic intake valve cleaning.

Ingenium engine, the infamous Ingenium.

born to replace the old 2.2 L diesel
engine, which in all fairness was a
decent enough engine. It had bags of

problem with that 2.2 though was, well,

little plastic particles, they
eventually find their way to the oil

I will say for those of you who already
own one of these, well, what do you do
beyond selling the bloody thing? Well,
the one of the best things you can do,
so long as that chain's not rattling
already, just keep changing that oil.
Keep changing the oil and filter, keep
fresh oil on that chain, keep flushing
out any of those plastic guide
particles, and that will go a long way
to prolonging that engine's life. The
other thing you can do is ensure that
that car is getting a good number of hot
motorway miles to complete DPF
regenerations. And and doing that,
you're going to limit the amount of oil
dilution that's taking place. So, making

will go a long long way as well. Sadly,

videos.transcript_text:
hello and welcome back to a new video on
my Channel today we will talk about the
Land Rover Discovery sport the discovery
sport has recently become very
affordable seven seater family car and
the Land Rover badge makes it more
appealing to Consumers I have dealt with
a dozen of these cars over the years and
I must say they are great cars to drive
and offer amazing Returns on miles per
gallon but you will need to be aware of
some of the issues that are common with
the discovery sport without further or
do let's dive in and share some of the
problems I have had with the discovery
sport the first common issues is to do
with the engenium engines that are
fitted to these SUVs these engines are
known to suffer from timing chain
failures and cause catastrophic engine
damages the quality of the timing chains
are very bad to the point that some of
the discovery Sports I owned had less
than 70,000 M on the odometer replacing
a loose timing chain is vital to saving
yourself thousands of pounds on a new
engine and generally you will be able to
tell a timing chain going bad by
listening to the engine when started
cold in the morning a rattling noise
coming from the back of the engine most
likely indicates a bad timing chain to
improve the lifespan of the timing chain
before it goes bad use premium oil
during oil changes and routine oil
changes must be carried out every 6 to
8,000
mil the second most problem I fa with
these SUVs was to do with bad gear
selectors for some unknown reason these
fancy looking gear selectors tend to
fail anytime anywhere without warning
which is very annoying and inconvenient
as it could leave you stranded away from
home and could cost you a fortune to
recover the car to a local garage the
only way to solve this issue is to buy a
new gear
selector the third issue I personally
had with the discovery sport was
inoperative door locks the door latches
or lock mechanisms are so poorly made
that it is only a matter of time before
they go bust and prevent you from
locking your Discovery sport in some
cases the door latch will set the alarm
off at the most inconvenient times
especially during early hours in the
morning the only solution to this issue
is to replace the door lock on the door
that fails to
lock the last issue that is to do with
the steering wheel system going bust a
failing power steering had happened on
three Discovery sports that I have had
and in one case the vehicle was doing
over 50 mph and suddenly the power
steering went and steering the car
became an impossible task luckily the
driver was able to pull away and stop
the car without causing an accident the
culprit to this problem is the bolts
that are holding the steering rack and
the steering motor together that rust
over time and weaken to the point that
they will break off there was a recall
on this problem for the early Discovery
Sports in the UK and the newer models
were fitted with stronger bolts to
prevent this from happening again the
points I have mentioned so far are my
own personal experience trading and
working with these cars over the past 4
years if you have faced other issues not
mentioned in this video please comment
your experience below it will be much
appreciated it's important to note that
these common faults can vary in severity
and frequency depending on the vehicle's
age mileage and how well it has been
maintained routine maintenance timely
repairs and using highquality parts and
fluids can help mitigate these issues
and ensure a longer trouble-free
ownership experience it's also advisable
to have a professional mechanic or Land
Rover dealership service your vehicle to
diagnose and address these issues
properly

The Nissan Qashqai J11 generation was first 
shown in 2013 and it also had a significant
facelift in 2017. In 2022 it was replaced with the 
new generation. Within 8 years of its existence,
the Qashqai managed to become one of the most 
popular SUVs in the UK and in Europe. But of
course, it came with a bunch of problems.
It’s impossible to cover all the issues
because this generation used 8 different engine 
models and each of them had some problems. But I
will focus on the most common issues that people 
talk about on forums and in Reddit threads. Also,
I asked several Nissan mechanics to give their 
opinions about this generation of the Qashqai.
So, among the engines, the 1.2-liter 
turbo engine seems to be one of the most
problematic. It has a chain that stretches 
until it reaches 150,000 kilometers. Also,
the flywheel is very weak and may require 
replacement before the car reaches 100,000
kilometers. The engine made between 2013 
and 2017 had electronic issues and there
are numerous software updates. But after 2017, 
the software issues were solved by Nissan.
This is a direct injection engine, so carbon 
buildup causes issues and requires cleaning.
Oil consumption is rather the feature 
of these engines, not a problem. Also,
these engines don’t last much longer than 
200,000 kilometers which is not that much at all.
Other engines including 1.3-liter turbo, 
1.6-liter turbo, 2.0-liter non-turbo,
and also 3 diesel engine models were much better 
in terms of common issues. They all share one
thing in common: you should change oil a little 
more often than Nissan recommends. Especially,
in the 1.5L diesel engine. Otherwise, 
problems will come earlier than you expect.
In terms of transmissions, this generation of 
the Qashqai offered wonderful 6-speed manual
transmissions. Basically, no problems with those. 
Some cars equipped with 1.2-liter turbo engines
had DCT transmissions after a facelift in 2017 and 
I would avoid those vehicles at all costs. Also,
the CVT is a disaster. All 3 types of Jatco 
CVT transmissions offered in the J11 generation
of the Qashqai are not long-lasting and are very 
expensive to repair. If you buy a used Nissan SUV,
just find a manual option or go for a low-mileage 
car with a good service history. The replacement
of this Jatco CVT will cost you about 7000 
euros while repairs are often impossible at all.
These Qashqai vehicles were assembled in the 
UK, in Sunderland, for European markets, so the
quality of assembly is quite good. But the thin 
paint is still there. The metal body parts are
protected from corrosion, so I haven’t seen rusty 
Qashqais even with big mileage on their odometers.
There is one problem in these Qashqai models: 
the wiper arms will damage the metal hood unless
you use the maintenance mode when installing new 
wiper blades. This is common for a lot of Nissan
vehicles now, so bear this in mind to avoid 
paint damage that is very expensive to repair.
Soundproofing is considered a problem in these 
vehicles. Well, this is a relatively inexpensive
SUV, so Nissan certainly didn’t spend a fortune 
on soundproofing materials and techniques. But I
wouldn’t say it’s so bad. And still, people 
in numerous forums complain about the noise
on highways. I would say that the quality of 
materials in the interior is the problem. If
you look inside the 10-year-old Qashqai, you 
will instantly see the consequences of this
low quality. Plastic parts don’t look fresh and

videos.title: GM 1.2L Turbo engine (LIH, LBP): Problems and life expectancy
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.2-liter 3-cylinder turbo engine 
is mainly used in the Buick Encore,
and also Chevy Trailblazer and Chevy Trax in 
the US. There are versions named LIH and LBP
and the only difference is that the LBP model is 
flex-fuel, so it can burn ethanol-based fuel with
no consequences. These engines are turbocharged 
and they offer pretty good power of 137 horsepower
and also impressive torque at 167 pound-feet.
But you are probably more interested in the
common issues with these engines. And since 
they have been made since 2019, we already know
a lot about their behavior after they reach 
100,000 miles or more, so there is a pretty
obvious understanding of the common problems.
First of all, I should point out that these
engines have a so-called wet timing belt. This 
is the belt that’s moved inside the engine and
works the same way as a chain would work. But it 
created less noise. And the problem with these
belts is that after about 50,000 miles, they start 
degrading and contaminating oil with their debris.
If such a belt is not replaced on time, it will 
clog the oil filter and eventually clog the oil
pump. When you see the oil pressure warning light 
on the dash of your Chevy or Buick equipped with
this engine, it’s most likely that the problem 
is huge and driving further is not a good idea.
The engine needs to be cleaned properly, 
otherwise you can kill it any minute. So,
I believe if you replace the belt here once 
every 40,000 miles, you’ll be good to go. Also,
the oil should only be used OEM because it affects 
the belt and any aftermarket oil may speed up the
process of belt degrading. Unfortunately, GM 
makes the same mistake as Ford and Citroen
with their wet-belt engine and recommends belt 
replacement at 150,000 miles. Well, I don’t think
a single 1.2 turbo engine will survive 150K miles 
without belt replacement. So keep an eye on it.
Other than that, these engines only have minor 
issues. They are pretty noisy and they vibrate
a little more than you would expect. Also, these 
engines have an overengineered start-stop system
that you will want to turn off every time you 
start your vehicle. And I’ve heard a lot of
complaints about the EVAP system throwing various 
warning lights and codes. But usually, those will
go away after some time causing no real harm.
One more important thing is that you shouldn’t
expect a lot of miles from this engine. I believe 
150,000 miles should be the average lifespan of
the 1.2-liter turbo since the engine only has 
3 cylinders and works with serious vibrations
all the time. After 100,000 miles, it will start 
consuming a little oil and at about 150,000 miles,
the engine may not be wise to repair since 
it’s about to end its short and bright life.

videos.title: Vauxhall 1.2 Turbo engine: Problems and key features
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.2-liter turbo engine in Vauxhall and Opel 
cars is actually the Peugeot EB2DTS engine.
Exactly the same engine is used in the Opel and 
Vauxhall Corsa F, Opel and Vauxhall Grandland X,
and also Peugeot 208, Peugeot 308, and Citroen C4. 
The slightly different variations of this engine
are also used in tons of other European cars 
that have connections with the Peugeot-Citroen
group. So, they are very popular and there are 
a lot of these engines on the road. By the way,
the engine was engineered back 
in 2014, so it’s not that fresh.
So, this is the 1.2-liter 3-cylinder 
turbocharged engine with direct injection,
the belt-driven timing system, and additional 
balance shafts in the block. The timing belt
is wet which means it’s located inside the engine 
and is submerged in oil bath. I will cover this a
little later in the problems section. The engine 
has a dual VTi valve timing system for efficiency
and economy. One more interesting thing 
is that the engine doesn’t have valve
lifters and you will have to adjust the 
valve clearance once every several years.
Interestingly, even in the Grandland X, 
the engine shows a pretty good dynamic
with its 130 horsepower. But the power is less 
important than torque which is pretty high here
at 240 Newton meters. Also, the engines are 
known for extremely good fuel economy. The
average combined city-highway consumption is 5.5 
liters per 100 kilometers or 51 MPG UK. Well,
it’s close to impossible to achieve these 
claimed figures in real life, but still,
it’s very impressive for an SUV.
So, when it comes to lifespan,
these engines are claimed to last about 250,000 
kilometers till you have first expensive repairs.
This is an average estimated lifespan, so 
some will drive these engines longer while
others may replace them at a lower mileage.
Opel and Vauxhall started using this engine in
2017, so they avoided having a bunch of 
initial problems. Earlier engine models
had issues with blocks and crankshafts 
but Peugeot fixed them pretty quickly.
One of the problems is the carbon buildup 
on intake valves because this is the direct
injection engine and fuel doesn’t travel 
through the valves, it’s directly injected
into the cylinders. Usually, the vehicles 
that are used mainly in city traffic have
carbon buildup issues after 50-60 thousand 
kilometers and require professional cleaning.
One more issue is the oil consumption that starts 
bothering owners at about 100,000 kilometers.
This means that oil rings on the pistons and 
valve seals start leaking a little oil into the
combustion chambers. While this is a relatively 
serious problem, there is nothing you can do to
prevent it. And fixing this issue will cost you 
a fortune, so owners usually keep adding oil and
driving further. You should keep an eye on the 
oil level because these engines won’t last even
a single day with critically low oil pressure.
But the worst issue is the wet-belt construction.
This is probably the worst timing system in 
the world of internal combustion engines. The
belt is pretty hard to replace that’s why labor 
costs are insane. The manufacturer says it will
last 180,000 kilometers. But it doesn’t last 
that much. While the belt most likely won’t
break and destroy the engine, it will start 
falling apart and contaminating your oil. The
parts of the belt material will travel to 
the filter and when the filter is clogged,
they will also be accumulated in the oil pump. At 
180,000 kilometers, when it’s time to change the
belt, it’s usually too late and the engine already 
suffers from poor oil pressure. You can avoid this
and I strongly recommend replacing the entire belt 
kit and cleaning the oil pump at about 100,000
kilometers or 6 years whatever comes first. And 
of course, you should only use the OEM kits.
They aren’t that expensive but the labor will be 
expensive, so there is no reason to save several
euros on the belt and compromise quality.
Overall, this is a well-engineered engine
with only one very serious problem with 
the wet timing belt. Other than that,
it’s pretty good to drive, very economical, and 
also relatively cheap to maintain and repair.

efficient dual clutch automatic gearbox
is Renault's dual clutch transmission
system designed to provide smooth and
fast gear changes while improving fuel
efficiency. How it works? The EDC system
works with two clutches. One for odd
gears, one, three, five, seven, and one
for even gears. 2 4 six reverse. When
the car is in a particular gear, the
next likely gear, either up or down, is
pre-selected on the other clutch. This
allows for near instantaneous shifts as
one clutch disengages while the other
engages simultaneously in which car is
installed. The EDC gearbox has been
widely installed across various Renault
models since its introduction around
2010. You can find it in Renault Cleo,
Renault Captor, Renault Megane,
including Megane GT and RS versions,
Renault Scenic/Grand Scenic, Renault
Talisman, Renault Codger, Renault Twingo
with certain engines, Renault Duster in

various engine configurations, including
TCE petrol and DCI diesel engines
versions. Renault utilizes different EDC

dry clutch often used in smaller lower

control module, TCM. Unusual noises and

insufficient lubrication and potential
damage if not addressed. Premature

misdiagnosis.

code? Well, it's a gear five incorrect
ratio. And so what does this mean? Well,
basically located on the transmission is
going to be an input speed sensor that's
monitoring the input shaft as it spins.
Then there's going to be an output speed
sensor that's monitoring the output
shaft of the transmission. And this
input shaft and output shaft will be
spinning at different RPMs depending on
what gear the transmission's in. But
when you get this P 0735 code, the
computer's seeing that there's some kind
of issue going on with the transmission
when it's in fifth gear, that the input
and output speed is outside the range
that should be and there's some kind of
issue going on there when the vehicle's
in fifth gear. And so it's going to be
troubleshooted to know why. And so what
would be some possible causes of a P 0
735 code? Well, the first thing that
could cause this is low fluid. really
dirty fluid or a clogged up filter
that's inside the transmission. So, the
first thing to go and do if possible is
go check the transmission fluid. Many
vehicles nowadays, they no longer let

problems. One thing to mention about

high miles on it and that fluid's never
been changed out. Quite often it's not a

fluid's never changed out and that

out the transmission fluid that's inside
the pan along with the filter.

been changed out and the transmission

like a week later, you get a lot of
other codes. But like I said, be sure to
do your own research on that since
opinions will vary. But the first thing

dirty fluid, or clogged up transmission

reporting bad information back to the
computer. So, the computer just thinks
there's a problem when there isn't. Of

just going to happen in fifth gear, and
you'll be getting like a Gear 3
incorrect ratio, gear 4 incorrect ratio.

a speed sensor code, like a P 0720
output speed sensor circuit or something
like that. And in this case, if you were
getting this code, then it's a good idea
to go test that output speed sensor and
check the wiring going to it. But the
next thing that could cause this is a
bad transmission sensor. And the next
thing that could cause this is that the
transmission's had some kind of failure
inside of it. It's got like a bad pump.
It's got a bad valve body, like a
selenoid's gone bad or something like
that. The transmission might had some
kind of failure. Again, usually that
happens. You'll be getting a lot of
other codes and you'll be getting like
fluid pressure codes, selenoid codes,
things like this. So, if you are getting
a lot of other codes, be sure to pay
attention to that because the next thing
that could cause this is some kind of
transmission failure. And the last thing
on list is going to be that there's some
kind of wiring issue or possibly the
computer's gone bad like the
transmission control module or
powertrain control module or something
like that. Basically, just keep in mind
that there's any kind of open short, a
blowing fuse, anything like this, then
that could cause problems. It's also
possible that there's a bad computer,
although that doesn't happen too often.
Usually, it's something else, but it
does happen sometimes. If you do think
you have a bad computer, be sure the
batteries charge good. You can even test
the alternator output and be sure that's
correct. Because all these computers,
they all need a good stable power supply
or that can cause problems and throw

weird things. But the last thing on list
