There are some things that drivers
inadvertently do that bring their diesel
engines closer to the point where it's
going to die or it's just going to break
down on them. In this video, we're just
going to look at some of the common
mistakes that drivers make with diesel
engines that are shortening the life of
that engine. The diesel engine has
always been regarded as solid,
agricultural, and bulletproof to some
extent.
Diesel engines do operate at lower RPM.
They produce lots of torque in this very
narrow power band because you get so
much low RPM torque. Many drivers lug
them. They ask too much of the engine.
Now, a diesel engine is fairly good at
delivering torque from low down, but we
still need to be sympathetic about our
gear selection. We don't want to put
unnecessary strain on the engine or the
transmission. And just choosing the
wrong gear can put that strain on the
engine or the transmission. We need to
be particularly sensitive. If we keep
stalling the car because we're in the
wrong gear or driving at the very lowest
RPM that we can reach is the most
economical point to drive at, we are
fooling ourselves. That is not true with
a diesel engine. And it's already got a
very narrow power band. So it makes a
lot of sense to fully exploit that power
band. And indeed, if we want the fuel
economy, we certainly need to be
exploiting the power band more fully
than just sitting at low RPM all the
time. Diesel fuel itself is a lubricant.
And this goes some way to explain why
diesel engines last so long. You
actually got diesel fuel, a lubricant,
going directly into the cylinders each
time the combustion process is taking
place. But that doesn't mean that we can
skip on servicing. The oil quality will
degrade. The oil will become diluted
over time as byproducts of the
combustion process and unburnt fuel seep
through. And that's particularly
something that's going to happen on cold
engines. If we do a lot of cold
journeys, the degradation on the oil
itself is certainly going to accelerate
and the oil is not going to do as good a
job of lubricating the engine. It's
important then to change the oil
regularly. Manufacturers may state 9,000
mi, 12,000 mi, or 12 months. But most
drivers who drive very, very high
mileage diesel engines cut those down.
They change the oil more frequently. And
that is the single biggest thing we can
do to prolong the life of our diesel
engine. The fuel system in a diesel
engine operates at extremely high
pressures up to 30,000 PSI. Poor quality
fuel, contaminants in the fuel, or just
faulty injectors can go a long way to
upset the smooth running of our diesel
engine. And now they come with
particulate filters. If the fuel is not
atomizing correctly as it burns, it's
producing more soot. And that soot is
going to clog up the particulate filter.
We need to be especially conscious of
the quality of the fuel that we use and
also the quality of the fuel system that
we've got in our car. If the injectors,
the fuel pump or any other components in
the fuel system are starting to degrade,
that can affect the running of the car,
we'll notice that initially with a drop
in MPG. It may be producing more soot.
That might lead to more common
regenerations of the particulate
filters. These are all signs that
something needs to be attended to within
our diesel engine. And ignoring that
will often cause the problem to
accelerate, to get bigger over time, and
we have a much more expensive repair to
deal with. We should never let the
diesel engine overheat if the coolant,
the thermostats, or there's any other
issue with the engine causing it to
overheat. That is a great way of killing
even a diesel engine. They are not
absolutely bulletproof. They are still
subject to the issues that come from an
overheating engine. Never ignore a
temperature gauge if it starts creeping
up above normal operating temperature
without a really good explanation. I.e.
we're driving through the Arizona desert
for example. Excessive idling. Now in
itself engines are designed to idle but
the idling process is very inefficient.
you're dumping a lot more moisture in
the oil components in the engine and
that leads to enhanced wear and tear
because the oil has now got water vapor
collecting in it. And at the idling
process, you may get more unburnt fuel
going through into the engine oil
itself. There's a lot of reasons why we
shouldn't idle an engine, a diesel
engine particularly, for long periods of
time. They can do it. They won't die if
we just do long periods of idling, but
we're degrading the oil and the wear and
tear on the engine is going to
accumulate faster if we have this habit
of allowing the engine to idle all the
time. You see a lot of delivery drivers
in vans and trucks, they just leave the
engine on all day long. The expense of
the wear and tear on the starter motor
will outweigh the saving that they would
make by shutting the engine off. But we
need to bear in mind as well that these
engines are hot all day long. They're
not doing the short journeys. They get
plenty of chance to burn off all of
these contaminants that have built up in
the oil itself. And that's probably why
a lot of these delivery drivers get away
with these excessively long idling
periods on their diesel engines. We see
a lot of issues that come about where
people delete the emission control
systems. They just blank off, say, the
EGR. They drill a big hole in the
particulate filter. These all reduce a
lot of the problems that they may have
been experiencing, which are often down
to poor maintenance or just the age of
the vehicle requiring a little bit more
care and attention. And in order to save
that expense, they've cut corners, but
they've not done it properly. Any
adjustment in the pollution control
systems requires an adjustment in the
ECU. If the engine is still expecting
these pollution control systems to be
operational, it's going to be getting
some very weird signals when they're not
operational, and that can lead to poor
running and further issues. Diesel
engines, like most engines, are
particularly sensitive to cold starts. A
lot more wear and tear happens during
the cold start, and we can offset a lot
of that by driving for a longer period
of time. We want to avoid those short
journeys on our diesel engines. If we
only ever do short journeys in our
diesel engines, that is going to lead to
all sorts of issues. The particulate
filter, for one, is not going to like
that. It's never going to get up to
temperature to burn off the particulates
it's collected, and that's going to lead
to blockages and poor running. Also, the
engine is not going to be as well
lubricated during these multiple cold
starts. The oil itself is going to
degrade. The chances of fuel dilution
happening is much greater on a cold
diesel engine than on a warm diesel
engine. If we're forced to do lots of
short journeys in our day-to-day work,
let's try and take the car for a run at
the weekend and let's shorten our
service intervals and get that oil
change. These are all ways of protecting
the longevity of our diesel engine. The
particulate filter regeneration needs
about 600° centigrade. That's about
1,112° F. And that only happens under
certain driving conditions. And the
regeneration process needs about 15 to
20 minutes. I've done other videos that
go into the regeneration process in more
detail. But if we never let this
regeneration process kick off or we
never let it fully complete, that is
going to lead to big problems, very
expensive problems further down the line
on our diesel engine. If you want to
know the signs to look out for as to if
the DPF regeneration is taking place,
I've done another video on that. So
check that out. I'll try and drop a link
into the description for that so you can
refer to that if that was something that
worried you. It's also good to check
regularly for error codes. Just plug in
your OBD reader into the OBD2 port on
the car and download any error codes and
diagnose them. That will give you an
early heads up to potential sensor
malfunctions or other issues that are
happening inside your diesel engine. And
by getting these early signs, you've
generally not always experienced
problems with the diesel engine itself,
and you can save yourself a breakdown or
a more expensive repair bill just by
nipping these things in the bud. So, I
really hope that this video has helped
you to get the best out of your diesel
engine. I've just highlighted a few of
the common diesel engine killers that I
see people doing all the time. And just
with a little bit of common sense, a
little bit of mechanical sympathy, we
can make our diesel engine last much
longer. Please boot the like button if

already. We'd hate you to miss out on
the great content we've got lined up.
And I've lined this video and this

help you to get the best out of your
diesel engine. Thanks for watching. See
you in these next videos.

videos.title: 5 Driving Habits That Ruin Your Diesel Engine (Without You Knowing)
videos.transcript_text:
Most diesel drivers have no idea they're
slowly destroying their engine just by
following a few common habits that seem
harmless. Diesel engines are powerful,
reliable, and built for longevity, but
only if you treat them right. The truth
is, your driving style can either make
your engine last 500,000 mi or ruin it
before it even hits 100,000.
So, in this video, I am revealing five
surprisingly common driving habits that
ruin your diesel engine, and most
drivers don't even know they're doing
them. If you drive a diesel, this is the
video you can't afford to skip. Let's
start with the first habit, frequent
short
trips. Diesel engines are designed to
run hot, and they need time to reach
full operating temperature to function
properly. But if you're constantly
making short trips, like running a few
miles to work, picking up groceries, or
dropping kids off at school, your engine
might never get hot enough. And that
creates problems, big ones. For
starters, it leads to carbon buildup in
the EGR system, which is responsible for
recirculating exhaust gases. Over time,
this buildup restricts air flow, reduces
performance, and eventually causes
engine trouble. That's not all. Short
trips also prevent the diesel
particulate filter, or DPF, from
properly regenerating. This means
unburnt fuel and soot accumulate in the
filter, causing clogs and back pressure.
And then there's your oil. If your
engine doesn't warm up, condensation and
unburnt fuel can mix with the oil,
degrading its ability to protect your
engine and increasing
wear. Bottom
line, short trips are a silent killer
for diesel engines. If you drive a
diesel, try to combine errands and take
longer drives to let your engine fully
warm up and do its job properly. The
second habit is letting your diesel idle
for long periods. Now, a lot of diesel
owners think idling is harmless or even
good for the engine. After all, trucks
idle all the time, right? But the truth
is, prolonged idling can do serious
damage. When your diesel engine idles
for too long, the fuel doesn't burn
efficiently. This leads to carbon
buildup on your pistons and injectors,
increasing wear and reducing
performance. It also causes soot to
accumulate in your DPF faster than
normal. requiring more frequent
regenerations or worse forcing expensive
replacements. But the biggest issue is
fuel dilution. At low RPMs, especially
during cold idling, fuel can seep past
the piston rings and into the engine
oil. This thins the oil out, reducing
its ability to lubricate and protect
engine components. Not good. So, if
you're stopped for more than a few
minutes, shut the engine off. It saves
fuel and extends your engine's life.
Habit number three is one that's
dangerously easy to overlook. A lot of
diesel drivers assume that because these
engines are built tough and because
modern synthetic oils are better, they
can go 10,000 to even 15,000 mi between
oil changes. And to be fair, that's
often what the dealer or manual
suggests. But here's the truth. If you
care about your diesel engine's
long-term health, that's way too long.
Diesel engines run hotter, harder, and
under much more stress than gas engines.
Your oil isn't just lubricating moving
parts. It's dealing with soot, fuel
dilution from idling, and chemical
byproducts from emission systems like
the EGR and DPF. Over time, these
contaminants build up and reduce your
oil's ability to protect the engine,
even if you're running top tier
synthetic. So, what's a smart oil change
interval? Stick to every 5,000 to 7,000
mi, especially if you're towing, doing
short trips, idling frequently, or
driving in dusty or harsh conditions.
That's the sweet spot for keeping your
engine clean and well lubricated. Don't
wait for your oil to look dirty. With
diesel engines, that happens quickly and
it's normal. The problem is what you
can't see. Microscopic wear, acidity,
and fuel dilution. Now, let's talk about
the fourth habit. Hard acceleration when
the engine is still cold. Picture this.
You start your diesel. It's been sitting
all night and the oil is cold and thick.
Then you jump on the highway and floor
it. What happens next isn't good. When
the engine is cold, the oil hasn't fully
circulated yet. That means critical
components like pistons, cylinder walls,
and the turbocharger are running without
proper lubrication. This can lead to
scoring, overheating, and long-term
wear. Not to mention, diesel engines
operate under high compression. So, the
added stress of full throttle
acceleration when things haven't warmed
up only makes matters worse. The turbo
especially takes a hit here. It spins at
extremely high speeds, and running it
hard before it's lubricated can
drastically shorten its lifespan. So,
what's the solution? Simple. Be gentle
with the throttle until your engine
reaches full operating temperature. That
gives the oil time to thin out and do
its job properly. It's a small change,
but it makes a huge difference. Habit
number five is one that even experienced
drivers often overlook. Not letting the
turbo cool down. After a long haul,
towing, or a high-speed drive, your
turbo is blazing hot. If you shut the
engine off immediately, the oil inside
the turbo essentially gets cooked. This
is called oil coing. And over time, it
creates hard carbon deposits that clog
oil passages, reduce cooling, and
destroy the turbo bearings. Once your
turbo goes, you're looking at a major
repair bill, easily into the thousands.
But here's the good news. It's easy to
avoid. Just let your engine idle for 30
to 60 seconds after hard driving. This
keeps oil flowing through the turbo and
lets it cool gradually, preventing coing
and protecting the turbo's
longevity. Some diesel vehicles have
turbo timers for this reason, but even
if yours doesn't, a short idle period
can make all the difference. Bonus habit
is ignoring fuel quality. Diesel fuel
isn't all created equal, and using poor
quality or contaminated diesel can
destroy your engine from the inside out.
Dirty fuel can clog injectors, damage
your high-pressure fuel pump, and fill
your filters with sludge. Water
contamination is especially dangerous.
It leads to corrosion in the fuel
system, and poor combustion. And don't
think fuel from every gas station is
safe. Some cut corners or have poorly
maintained tanks. That's why it's
important to buy diesel from reputable
stations, use fuel additives if
necessary, and regularly drain your
water separator. Diesel engines rely on
clean pressurized fuel to run properly.
So, make sure you're giving them the
best. These five habits, short trips,
excessive idling, hard acceleration when
cold, shutting down a hot turbo, and
using poor fuel might seem minor, but
they're some of the biggest reasons
diesel engines fail early. The good news
is they're all avoidable. Treat your
diesel with care, and it will reward you
with performance, power, and long life.
And there you have it, the five driving
habits you need to avoid if you want
your turbo diesel to last. If you found
this helpful, make sure to hit the like
button and subscribe for more diesel
maintenance tips. Thanks for watching.
And if you made it this far, I
appreciate you.

this part controls the flow of the oil

found near your engine either on the

cylindrical part with an electrical
connector on one end and a metal housing
that goes into the engine now let's get
started symptom number one rough idling
the engine May idle roughly or
inconsistently when your VVT solenoid
isn't working right this happens because
the solenoid controls the oil flow that
adjusts when your engine valves open and
close so when the solenoid fails the
timing gets off which causes the engine
to misfire or have trouble keeping a
steady idle eventually leading to rough
or uneven idling symptom number two loss
of power when your VVT solenoid goes bad
you might also notice a loss of power

openings and closings gets off this
makes it harder for the engine to get
the right mix of air and fuel which
reduces its
efficiency as a result your engine can't
produce as much power especially when

engine stalling a bad VVT solenoid can
cause engine stalling because again it
affects the timing of your engines
valves when the solenoid fails it may
not allow the oil to flow properly
leading to incorrect valve timing this
creates an imbalance in the air and fuel
mixture causing the engine to run poorly

keeping power especially at low speeds

stalling if if this happens it can make

on the bonnet release lever and open the bonnet.
Take off the engine cover.

You will now be able to see the various elements 
to remove so that you can access the injectors.

For safety reasons, we recommend unplugging the 
battery. Using a socket wrench and a 10m socket,

unscrew the terminal from the 
negative terminal. Now remove it.

Using a Phillips screwdriver, unscrew the 
clamping clip on the air inlet conduit.

Pull upwards to free it.
You will then have to remove

the metallic duct. To do this, you will have 
to remove the pin that holds it in place. You

can see how it works in these images. Use the 
flathead screwdriver to lever and remove it.
Using a socket wrench and a 6mm Allen socket,

remove the last holding screw 
on the conduit, then remove it.

So that impurities do not fall into the duct, 
cover the opening with a piece of tissue.

Using a socket wrench and a 10mm socket, now 
unscrew the two screws on the plastic protection.

Then unclip the electricity 
casing on the plastic protection.
Release the two latches.

Unscrew and remove the air inlet conduit. 
Then remove the plastic protection.

You now have access to the 4 injectors. The 
numbers of the injectors are important. The number

one is located on the gear box side, whereas 
number four is located on the drive belt side.
To facilitate the removal of the injectors,

start by unplugging the glow plug 
located next to the injector.

You then need to move the oil gauge out of the way 
by unscrewing the two holding screws that hold it

in place using a socket wrench and an 8mm socket.
Shift the gauge.

You can also disconnect the injector 
by pushing down on the plastic tab

and by pushing with the flathead 
screwdriver all while pulling upwards.

Using a flathead screwdriver push the woodruff key 
that locks the plastic fuel return hose in place.
Then using needle nose pliers remove it.
Remove the plastic fuel return hose.
Using a 17mm spanner, start releasing the two ends

of the tubing which links the 
injection bar to the injector.
Now finish off the removal of the tubing.

The injectors and the injection 
bar are extremely fragile parts.

We recommend protecting them so that 
no impurity can enter the system.

Using a socket wrench, an 
extender and a 10mm socket,

unscrew the fixing flange on 
the injector and remove it.

If there is a leak from the injector seal, it can 
be difficult to remove as it will be glued down.

The injector may be blocked, do 
not hesitate to use penetrating oil

and a 11mm spanner to make rotating 
movement and take it out of its housing.

but it is often block at the bottom of the shafts.

You have to try and unstick it by alternating 
clean deposits which hold it and putting it

under tension with a thin screwdriver. Be 
careful no to scratch the injector shafts.

Before installing the new injector,

and in particular the part that is in contact with 
the seal. We recommend attaching a small plastic

tube to the vacuum cleaner so that it doesn't 
fall into the combustion chamber. you can also

from your vehicle. Without reprogramming it,

videos.transcript_text:
Hey guys, Jake with 8020 Media here.
Today we're doing a video on common
problems and reliability issues with GM's
2.4-liter EcoTec inline four engine.
The 2.4 EcoTec was released in
2006 and used all the way through
2017 across GM's line of vehicles,
including Chevy, GMC, Buick, Saturn,
and Pontiac,
and was used through 2019
in the Polaris Slingshot.
The 2.4 EcoTec is a small,
naturally aspirated inline four
that produces anywhere from
164 to 182 horsepower.
While it doesn't offer a whole
lot in terms of performance,
it does offer a lot in terms of
fuel economy and gas mileage.
Throughout the 11-year
span of the 2.4 EcoTec,
it went through a number of
different revisions in generations.
There were six different engine
variants that were produced within the
lifespan of the 2.4 EcoTec.
So we look at the six different
engine variations here.
There's really two subsets of it.
The original engine was the LE5,
and then from there they built two
different variations of the LE5.
One of them was the LAT,
which was essentially the
same thing as the LE5,
but it was the version that was used in
hybrid vehicles. And then you had the
LE9, which was an E85
compatible version of the LE5.
So that kind of covers it for the
first subset of the 2.4 EcoTec.
And then the second one
starts with the LAF.
This was a new 2.4 design
that used a very similar
base engine design,
but switched to direct
injection from port injection.
They increased the compression and
they also redesigned the pistons.
After the LAF, they produced an LEA,
which was the same thing as the
LAF, but was flex-fuel capable.
And then there was the LUK,
which was the same as the LEA,
but added eAssist to it. All of these
engines are very similar in design.
The first three variations are very
similar to the last three variations,
with the exception of the direct
injection, the higher compression,
and the different pistons.
Jumping into common problems and
reliability with these engines.
Overall,
these engines have somewhat of
a poor reputation online for
reliability. There's only four
problems that we're gonna discuss here.
However, there are two main problems,
and that's timing chain failure
and excessive oil consumption,
which are part of what has given
this engine a bad reputation online.
I will say I think the Internet's blown
it a little bit out of proportion,
but timing chain failure still
is a relatively common problem
on these engines.
It seems to mostly affect the Equinox
and Malibu vehicles for whatever
reason, but essentially,
the timing chain tensioner and the upper
bolt that holds it in are problematic,
which causes the timing chain tensioner
to fail. And when the tensioner fails,
it leads to some serious internal
damage because the 2.4 EcoTec
is an interference engine,
so it essentially causes the
valves to collide with each other.
In a worst-case scenario,
you're gonna have to completely replace
all of the valves within the engine,
which is going to essentially require
a pretty material rebuild of it. Now,
the timing chain does tend
to develop slack over time,
and so sometimes you will notice some
noise going on within the timing chain.
If you hear any of that,
we recommend replacing the timing chain
just because you don't want to end up
running into any issues with
the tensioner, later on,
that can cause serious
internal damage. Now,
the timing chain on these vehicles tends
to fail around the 100,000-mile mark.
We recommend replacing the timing chain
once you get around that 100,000-mile
mark, or if you hear any noises
within the timing chain before then.
Now the tensioner can fail instantaneously
to where you don't have any
signs leading up to it. That can cause
some significant damage internally,
and that's one of the main reasons that
these engines have a bad reputation.
Like I said, I think it's been blown
out of proportion a little bit,
but it still is a common enough
problem for it to give us a
little bit of concern with these engines
and probably knock it down on our
rating scale with respect to reliability.
Now the second problem is with
excessive oil consumption.
This also tended to affect the Equinox
and the Malibu more so than the other
engines,
and I think is also part of the reason
that those vehicles had as many issues
with the timing chains
as they did. Essentially,
there was a poor design
with the piston rings,
and this is mostly for
2010 to 2013 models,
but the piston rings had a poor design,
which allows a lot of
oil to seep past them,
and then the oil's burned off
within the combustion chamber.
And essentially what this causes
is oil loss with no visible
signs of oil leaking within the engine
or onto the floor in your driveway.
There was a class action lawsuit around
this just because of the number of
vehicles that this affected and all those
vehicles were able to get an extended
warranty to get the piston rings
repaired to fix issues with excessive oil
consumption. On most of the
vehicles out there, hopefully,
this repair has been done,
but just something to be cautious of
if you are looking at buying one. The
reason that this is tied
in with the timing chain
problems is one of the easiest
ways to blow up your timing
chain is to starve it of oil.
When you run into issues with
excessive oil consumption,
the engine loses oil over time,
and that can starve the timing chain and
timing chain components of the oil that
they need to operate, which could
then lead to timing chain failure.
So those are the two major
problems on these engines.
A couple other ones are carbon buildup.
Carbon buildup only affects the LAF, LEA,
and LUK engine variants, which are
the ones that have direct injection.
Because with direct injection,
the fuel is shot directly into the
combustion chamber rather than into the
intake ports. And so what happens is
carbon deposits form across the intake
valves,
which restricts airflow and essentially
limits the amount of space for air,
and so it can, over time,
lead to the slow decline in performance.
If you have really bad carbon buildup,
you might get some misfires
and some rough idling. However,
this is typically a problem that you
don't even notice is occurring because the
buildup happens slowly over time,
so you'll just slowly lose power over
time rather than having noticeable change
in performance instantaneously,
or at one point in time.
Carbon buildup isn't really
that serious of a problem.
It'll slowly zap some performance,
but it really doesn't do a whole lot
beyond that if it gets really bad,
some chunks of carbon can pass through
the valves and get into the combustion
chamber and cause problems,
but that's pretty rare.
We do recommend trying to clean the intake
valves through walnut blasting every
80,000 to 120,000 miles. We do have a
video on our channel about how to walnut
blast your vehicle. If you
don't know what that is,
check that out because that's the
best way to clean your intake valves.
Jumping into the last problem,
it's kind of a more generic one,
but it's oil leaks.
The 2.4 EcoTec has a couple components
that are prone to leaking oil more than
others, like the valve cover
gasket, the oil pan gasket,
and the main seal.
This is really more of a higher
mileage maintenance item.
You're probably not going to see
oil leaks on any sub 100,000-mile
cars that have been taken care of.
And so this is typically something that
occurs in vehicles that are 10 plus
years old and sometimes ones that
weren't properly taken care of,
but also ones that have just been driven
a lot and have worn down over time. All
of these gaskets, the oil pan,
valve cover, and main seal,
are relatively difficult to replace,
and so while the gaskets for
them are probably $20 or $30,
the labor cost to actually replace
them is gonna be a bit more expensive.
Maintenance wise, when you do have
an oil leak from one of these spots,
it can be a little bit expensive to fix.
So that covers it for the common
problems on this vehicle. Overall,
this engine probably gets very
average grade for reliability.
Most of the problems really tend to
be seen on the Equinox and Malibu,
as well as from 2010 to 2013,
but that is not to say that the problem
was only with the Equinox and Malibu.
All of the vehicles that had the
2.4 EcoTec in it did have cases of
timing chain failure,
as well as issues with excessive oil
consumption. It was just the Equinox and
Malibu that got the
warranty, or the recall,
for the piston rings. While it
is more prone on those cars,
it certainly still is prone
on all of the other ones.
Maintenance is the key on these engines.
You can make it to the 200,000-mile mark,
but that definitely requires proper care
and maintenance as well as a little bit
of luck and probably replacing the timing
chain two or three times to make sure
you do get there because that is the one
thing that will send this engine to the
grave a lot sooner than
it should go to the grave.
That covers it for this video. If you
guys appreciate it, please like the video,
subscribe to our channel and
stay tuned for more GM content.

videos.title: How to Renew manual transmission oil on the Renault Megane 2008 to 2014
videos.transcript_text:
this free step-by-step video comes to
you directly from haynes
you can complete more than 200 jobs on
this vehicle when you purchase the
complete hanes online manual at
hanes.com
this operation is much quicker and more
efficient if the car is first taken on a
journey of sufficient length to warm the
engine and gearbox up to operating
temperature
jack up the front and rear of the car
and support it on axle stands the car
must be level for the check to be
accurate
remove the engine undershield
draining
locate the drain plug at the bottom of
the gearbox remove all traces of dirt
from around the drain and filler stroke
level plugs
place a suitable container underneath
the drain plug to catch the used gearbox
fluid
remove the plug with the appropriate
size square drive and allow the fluid to
be drained completely
if the oil is hot take precautions
against scolding
when the oil has finished draining clean
the drain plug threads and those of the
gearbox casing
fit a new seal to the drain plug
fit the drain plug and tighten it to 24
newton meters
refilling and checking locate the
plastic filler stroke level plug and
clean the area around it before removal
the plug is located close to the
left-hand drive shaft on the six-speed
gearbox models
unscrew and remove the plug this could
be very tight
check the condition of the filler plug
seal and obtain a new one if necessary
add fluid using the specified type of
lubricant until the gearbox oil level is
correct
access to the filler plug on the
six-speed gearbox is limited we used a
large syringe and a length of tubing
fill the gearbox until oil starts to
flow out and allow excess oil to drain
out completely
the oil level should be up to the lower
edge of the filler stroke level plug
aperture
once the oil level is correct refit the
filler stroke level plug and tighten it
securely by hand only
note that frequent need for topping up
indicates a leak possibly through an oil
seal the core should be investigated and
rectified
refit the engine undershield
lower the car to grind
you

videos.title: 1.3 TCE REVIEW, PROBLEMS, RELIABILITY, FAILURES, FUEL CONSUM, TIMING, OIL?
videos.transcript_text:
Welcome to the Automoto Freak channel.
Greetings to all viewers, subscribers,
supporters. So, to the point, the
Renault 1.3 TCE engine known by its
internal code H5H Renault or M282
Mercedes-Benz is a relatively modern
four-cylinder turbocharged gasoline
engine that was co-developed by the Rena
Nissan Mitsubishi Alliance and Daimler
Mercedes-Benz. Introduced around 2018,
it replaced the problematic 1.2TC
H5F and aimed to set new standards in
performance, efficiency, and reliability
for compact gasoline engines. It's
widely used across a broad range of
vehicles. Renault Cleo V Chapter 2 Meane
4 Kajger Arana
Scenic Grand Scenic DEA Duster Logan
Sandere Nissan Kosk Juke X-Trail
MercedesBenz Aclass B-Class CLA GLA GB
or it's known as the M282
review and opinions. Generally, the
1.3TCE
has received a much more positive
reception than its 1.2TCE predecessor.
Performance. It's praised for its strong
performance across various power
outputs. Typically 115HP,
140HP,
150HP, and 160hp/
163HP. The direct injection and
turbocharging provide good low-end
torque, making vehicles feel responsive
and capable even on highways.
Refinement, it's generally considered
smooth and quiet, especially compared to
many three-cylinder engines. Efficiency,
it's designed with fuel efficiency and
lower CO2 emissions in mind, making it
competitive in its class. Collaboration.
The fact that it's a joint venture with
Daimler is often seen as a positive,
implying higher engineering standards
and rigorous testing. Advantages: Good
power and torque. Offers robust
performance for its size, making it
suitable for a variety of vehicle types
from compact cars to smaller SUVs.
Responsive driving. Thanks to direct
injection and an electrically controlled
turbocharger, it delivers power smoothly
and quickly. Fuel efficiency. Despite
its good performance, it maintains
competitive fuel consumption figures.
Advanced technologies features like
mirror bore coating, a cylinder coating
technology for reduced friction and
improved heat conduction inspired by the
Nissan GTR engine. Increased fuel
pressure up to 250 bar and dual variable
valve timing VVT contribute to its
efficiency and performance. Timing chain
utilizes a timing chain which is
generally designed for the life of the
engine, reducing maintenance costs
compared to a timing belt.
Disadvantages. Direct injection
specifics. As with all direct injection
engines, there's a potential for carbon
buildup on intake valves over very high
mileage. Though modern designs like the
1.3TC aim to mitigate this GPF gasoline
particulate filter many versions
especially in Europe come with a GPF to
meet emission standards. While necessary
GPF can be a source of potential issues
if the car is used predominantly for
short trips which might prevent proper
regeneration cycles. Complexity being a
turbocharged direct injection engine
with advanced features. It is more
complex than older, simpler engines,
potentially leading to higher repair
costs if issues do arise. Common faults
and breakdowns. Compared to the 1.2TCE,
the 1.3TCE
H5H/M282
has a much better reliability record.
However, no engine is entirely
fault-free. Thermostat housing issues.
Some early reports, particularly from
Mercedes M282 owners, mentioned issues
with the plastic thermostat housing
breaking at the seam, leading to coolant
leaks and potential overheating if not
addressed. This seems to be one of the
more consistently reported weak points.
Occasional oil consumption. While not
widespread like the 1.2TCE,
there have been very isolated reports of
higher thanex expected oil consumption.
This is often tied to driving style or
neglected maintenance rather than a
fundamental design flaw. Turbocharger
issues. A few isolated cases of
turbocharger failures have been
reported. Similar to any turbocharged
engine, often linked to aggressive
driving or insufficient oil changes.
Vibrations/noise
at idle. Some users have noted minor
vibrations or noise at idle, which can
be characteristic of small capacity
engines, but usually not indicative of a
major fault. Fuel consumption. The 1.3TC
engine is generally efficient for its
power output. Real world fuel
consumption depends heavily on the
vehicle it's in, driving style, and
transmission. For a Renault Meane 1.3TC
140, users report averages ranging from
6.0 0 to 7.5 L/100 km for mixed driving.
For a heavier vehicle like the Kajger
1.3TC
140, averages might be around 7.0 to 8.0
L/100KM.
On highways, it's capable of achieving
figures below 6.0 L/100
km. While in heavy city traffic, it can
go above 8.0 L/100 km. Timing. The
Renault 1.3TCE
H5H/M282
engine uses a timing chain. This is a
significant advantage over engines with
timing belts as chains are generally
designed to last the life of the engine
and do not require periodic replacement.
This greatly reduces long-term
maintenance costs and concerns. Oil. Oil
type. The recommended engine oil for the
1.3 tce H5H/M282
typically conforms to Renault RN17 or
Mercedes-Benz MB 229.52
specifications. These usually correspond
to ACSC3
for RN17 and often have a viscosity of
5W30. For some variants, especially
those requiring lower viscosity for fuel
economy, Renault RN17 FE ACSC5 with a 0W
20 viscosity might be specified. Oil
capacity. The oil capacity generally
ranges from 5.0 to 5.5 L depending on
the specific vehicle model and engine
variant. Eg 5.5 L for Renault Captor
1.3TC150.
Importance of correct oil. Given the
engine's direct injection and
turbocharging, using the correct
specification and high quality oil is
paramount for its longevity and
performance, especially to minimize
carbon deposits and ensure proper
lubrication of the turbocharger and
timing chain. change intervals adhering
to the manufacturer's recommended oil
change intervals often 20,000 kilometers
or annually or 10,000 m/12 month for
Mercedes-Benz is important. However, for
those who drive in harsher conditions,
eg frequent short trips, heavy traffic,
more frequent oil changes, eg every
10,000 km or 6 months could be
beneficial. Overall, the Renault 1.3TCE
H5H/M282
engine is a significant step up from its
predecessor, offering a much more
balanced combination of performance,
efficiency, and so far improved
reliability. Its joint development with
Daimler instills confidence, and a use
of a timing chain is a welcome feature.
While no engine is without its
occasional quirks, the widespread
systemic issues of the 1.2TC and 2TCE do
not appear to be present in the 1.3TC.
It's generally considered a good choice
for those seeking a modern, economical,
and capable gasoline engine in Renault,
DEA, Nissan, or Mercedes-Benz vehicles.
As with any modern turbocharged direct
injection engine, diligent adherence to
service schedules and using the correct
highquality lubricants are crucial for
its long-term health. Thank you for
watching the video and I invite you to
subscribe to the Automotoreak channel.
Greetings to everyone and see you in the
next episode. See you soon.

Tag Questions – English Grammar Lessons
videos.transcript_text:
Ellii
Tag Questions
What are tag questions?
Tag questions include a short phrase, called the “tag,” 
at the end of a positive or negative sentence stem.
For example, in the question 
“That was a good movie, wasn’t it?”
“that was a good movie” is the sentence 
stem, and “wasn’t it?” is the tag.
Why do we use tag questions in English?
We use tag questions for emphasis or confirmation.
Tag questions are very common in spoken English.
When we are sure that someone will agree with 
what we are saying, we can use a tag question.
For example, if my friend and I are looking 
at a small kitten and I think it is cute,
I would assume that my friend 
also thinks it is cute.
I can ask, "That kitten is cute, isn’t it?" and 
my friend will probably answer, “Yes, it is!”
How do we form tag questions in English?
Look at the position of the subject 
and verb in the sentence stem.
Then form the tag by reversing the order.
In other words, put the verb 
before the subject in the tag.
For example, in the question “She is tired, isn’t she?" 
the subject “she” comes before the verb “is” in the stem.
In the tag, the verb “isn’t” 
comes before the subject “she.”
The tag always takes a subject pronoun.
If the subject in the sentence stem of the question
 is a pronoun, it remains the same in the tag.
If the subject in the stem is a noun, 
it becomes a pronoun in the tag.
For example, in the question 
“They are hungry, aren’t they?”
the subject of the stem is “they,” so 
the subject of the tag doesn’t change.
But in the question “The children 
are hungry, aren’t they?”
the subject of the stem is “children,” so 
the subject of the tag changes to “they.”
The tag verb is always opposite 
of the verb in the sentence stem.
If the verb in the stem is 
positive, the tag is negative.
If the verb in the stem is 
negative, the tag is positive.
For example, in the question “He 
speaks French fluently, doesn’t he?”
the verb in the stem is positive, 
so the verb in the tag is negative.
But in the question “He doesn’t 
speak Spanish fluently, does he?”
the verb in the stem is negative, 
so the verb in the tag is positive.
If the sentence stem uses the Be 
verb, the tag uses the Be verb too.
For example:
This pasta is delicious, isn't it?
The baseball game wasn’t canceled, was it?
If the sentence stem uses a simple present verb other 
than Be, the tag uses “don’t,” “do,” “doesn’t,” or “does.”
For example:
You like ice cream, don’t you?
They don’t like broccoli, do they?
He likes pasta, doesn’t he?
If the sentence stem uses a simple past verb 
other than Be, the tag uses “didn’t” or “did.”
For example:
We ran for hours in gym class, didn’t we?
You didn’t finish your homework, did you?
For all other tenses and modals, the tag uses the 
auxiliary verb or modal that was used in the sentence stem.
For example:
Your neighbors have sold 
their house, haven’t they?
She will call me back, won’t she?
You can’t play the guitar, can you?
What is intonation?
“Intonation” refers to the rising 
or falling sound of someone’s voice.
For tag questions, we use rising intonation in the tag when 
we are about 80–90% sure that someone will agree with us.
We use falling intonation in the tag when we are 
about 95% sure that someone will agree with us.
For example, if my friend and I watched a really good 
action movie, but I know my friend prefers comedies,
then I’m only about 80–90% sure 
that my friend will agree with me.
In this case, I would use rising intonation.
I would say, "That was a great movie, wasn’t it?"
But if I know my friend loves 
action movies as much as I do,
then I’m about 95% sure that my friend will 
agree with me, so I would use falling intonation.
I would say, "That was a great movie, wasn’t it?"
How do we respond to tag questions in English?
Make sure you respond to the 
sentence stem, not the tag.
If you agree with the sentence stem, use the 
same type of verb in your response as the stem.
Respond with “yes” for a positive 
sentence and “no” for a negative sentence.
For example:
You like hot weather, don’t you?
Yes, I do. I like hot weather.
You don’t like cold weather, do you?
No, I don’t. I don’t like cold weather.
If you disagree with the sentence stem,  use the 
opposite type of verb in your response as the stem.
Respond with “no” for a positive sentence 
and “yes” for a negative sentence.
For example:
You like hot weather, don’t you?
No, I don’t. I don’t like hot weather.
You don’t like cold weather, do you?
Yes, I do. I like cold weather.
Look at the picture and the sentence stem.
Say or write the correct tag.
Try saying each question twice.
First, imagine you are 80–90% sure that someone 
will agree with you and use rising intonation.
Then imagine you are 95% sure that someone 
will agree with you and use falling intonation.
For example:
You don’t feel well today, do you?

What are tag questions?

Tag questions include a short phrase, called the “tag,” 
at the end of a positive or negative sentence stem.

For example, in the question

Why do we use tag questions in English?
We use tag questions for emphasis or confirmation.
Tag questions are very common in spoken English.

When we are sure that someone will agree with 
what we are saying, we can use a tag question.

For example, if my friend and I are looking 
at a small kitten and I think it is cute,

I would assume that my friend 
also thinks it is cute.

I can ask, "That kitten is cute, isn’t it?" and 
my friend will probably answer, “Yes, it is!”
How do we form tag questions in English?

Look at the position of the subject 
and verb in the sentence stem.
Then form the tag by reversing the order.

In other words, put the verb 
before the subject in the tag.

For example, in the question “She is tired, isn’t she?" 
the subject “she” comes before the verb “is” in the stem.

In the tag, the verb “isn’t” 
comes before the subject “she.”
The tag always takes a subject pronoun.

If the subject in the stem is a noun, 
it becomes a pronoun in the tag.

For example, in the question 
“They are hungry, aren’t they?”

the subject of the stem is “they,” so 
the subject of the tag doesn’t change.

are hungry, aren’t they?”

the subject of the stem is “children,” so 
the subject of the tag changes to “they.”

entire used vehicles cost. If you catch

videos.title: used VW Golf MK6 (5K1) - 2008-2013, Complete Buying guide with Common Issues
videos.transcript_text:
The 6th generation VW Golf is a perfect daily driver,
until one of the magnificent tsi engines break.
But let’s not overtake the things which 
should not be overtaken.
This Mk6 Golf is just sort of a facelift of the older Mk5 since 
they share the same platform and what not.
Besides the 3 or 5 door hatchback there is also 
the more practical wagon,
if you need that extra space for your dog, fridge, oven or wardrobe and what not.
There is also the convertible, the Jetta and the Golf plus, but I’m not going to mention these anymore,
because the universe would not handle that much information.
The interior of this Golf is a typical Golf interior, so it can be equipped poorly but also pretty damn well
other than this:
-the build quality is good, although some rattles can occur mainly from the doors or B pillar area
-the space is good, although it’s still a small car so don’t expect miracles
-the materials quality is good, although there are occasionally cases of sagging headliner in cars used in hot climate areas
-and lastly the ergonomics is great, but there are more important things to mention so for more information about the interior visit my website.
Overall the body is protected well from the rust, however on cars used regularly on winter salty roads,
it’s definitely worth to check for rust on 3 places:
-the front fenders can rust
-the front edge of the sills can rust, because over time dirt builds up in this area behind the wheel well liner
-and lastly there is the tailgate which can rust mostly around 
the 3rd brake light, but sometimes on the edges, around the middle drain hole
+ occasionally around the VW badge too, so basically check the whole damn tailgate for rust!
But let’s move on to the minor issues unrelated to engine or gearbox,
so: -the trunk door lock can fail more often causing the trunk door not to lock properly, or it will be stuck in closed position
-excessive tail light condensation can occur too, in the outer as well as in inner tail lights
-then there is the AC system which you should check properly since:
the AC compressor clutch hub can wear out,
the AC condenser can leak more often,
the blower motor resistor can fail
and the air recirculation flap motor located behind the glove box can break too.
Then of course check the functionality of the other regular stuff like the power windows, door locks, rear and front windscreen wipers and all that other shit as usual.
For more information and for guides how to fix these issues visit my website!
As the other cars, this Golf can also have issues with various water leaks into the interior,
so check the footwell area and the trunk spare tire area for traces of water.
There are numerous sources of water leaks, but let’s start with the rear of the car, specifically with the tailgate,
so:  -the inner tail light seals can let the water in
+ in this case there should be a visible condensation in them
-next the 3rd brake light can let the water in
-then occasionally the draining tube of the rear badge can be dislodged and drain the water into the trunk
+let’s not forget the plastic washer fluid pipe which can crack,
usually in this wiring loom rubber grommet and in this case it obviously leaks washer fluid into the interior or into the tailgate.
Moving on to the front of the car:
-the 2 water drains under the windshield on the sides of the scuttle area can be clogged letting the water to accumulate here,
and leak into the interior thru the plastic air inlet.
-then the ac drain in the front right footwell can leak
-and also the rear windscreen washer plastic pipe can crack and leak washer fluid,
again in the front right passenger footwell area.
Additionally if the car is equipped with a sunroof then you can easily get another leak from the sunroof drains.
There are 4 drain hoses in each corner of the sunroof frame.
The rear drain hoses are usually fine, but the front drain hose rubber endings can be often clogged.
To access these drain endings you have to remove the windscreen wipers and the plastic panel,
since the front drain hoses drain the water into this scuttle area.
However sometimes the drain hose can also disconnect from this rubber grommet
which goes thru the firewall-and in this case you 
again end up with water in the front footwell.
But I’m not finished yet, since the estate models 
can be equipped with a big panoramic sunroof
which also has 4 drains. But in this case you can 
easily get a leak from all of these drain hoses,
since all of them have badly designed upper drain 
connections.
These connectors glued to these hoses simply get a little loose over time creating a gap around the hose which allows the water to leak not just into,
but also onto the drain hose and into the interior.
+ of course the front drains can  get clogged the same way as on the regular sunroof.
This Golf was available with the standard suspension, with the factory sport suspension or with the electronically adjustable suspension.
As always check for all those knocking, 
clunking or rattling noises from the suspension
and keep in mind that the electronic shocks are 
obviously more expensive than the regular type.
From the petrol engines the most reliable are the 
older 1.4 l and 1.6 l naturally aspirated units.
They are not very powerful and also not 
that economical as the newer engines,
but they can easily withstand 300 000 km or 
more with regular maintenance only.
However it’s worth mentioning that after approx. 200 
000 km or 250 000 km you can experience bigger or smaller oil consumption.
+ of course let’s not forget about the 2.5 l 5 cylinder engine available in the US,
which is also a great, reliable and a fairly simple unit,
so all I can say is: Buy it if you can!
But from now on it’s going to be nothing but downhill on a highway to hell…
So let me introduce you the newer TSI- totaler, schrottmotor inclusive,
turbocharged and direct injection engines which are powerful enough while achieving a good fuel consumption,
But they can have numerous, numerous issues:
-let’s start with the 1.2 l TSI
The biggest issue of this smallest engine can be with the timing chain mechanism which is made from boiled potatoes basically.
It’s because in plenty of cases it was and it can 
be worn even before 100 000 km, and in fact
The next problem of this tiny engine can be with the faulty turbo wastegate actuator,
but in this case the actuator arm can be only stuck, so before replacing the actuator itself,
its worth to first disassemble the actuator and try to free up the things.
The last issue worth mentioning is that this engine is more prone to oil dilution with fuel.
So if you will use this engine for very short distances only, then you can experience that the fuel will slowly get into the oil
which is not very good in the long term.
-the 1.4 l TSI with 122 hp is on the other hand a much better engine,
but even this unit can have issues with the prematurely worn timing chain.
In this case you can expect this issue mostly between 
100 000 km and 150 000 km. However,
in some cases the chain mechanism can be worn even before 100 000 km, but again mostly in the cars made to 2011.
-next there is the infamous 1.4 l TSI with 160 hp,
which is equipped with a turbocharger and also with a compressor to achieve the very good performance.
But the various possible issues of this engine are not that good as the performance.
And again let’s start with the damn timing chain, which as in the previous engine can be worn mostly between 100 000 km and 150 000 km,
but there are also cases of worn chain mechanism even before 100 000 km mainly in cars made to 2011.
The next issue of this engine is related to the compressor, specifically to the magnetic clutch of the compressor,
which can fail even before 100 000 km causing weak engine performance,
since the compressor is not gonna be to be engaged.
In this case you will have to replace this clutch which is connected to the water pump.
But let’s move onto the most interesting issue this engine can have which is related to the pistons.
Specifically the side of the pistons can crack
and also break off basically, even before 100 000 km.
This will cause misfires because of low compression, excessive oil consumption, a check engine light can be also present of course,
and also some other funny shit.
Replacing the pistons and all the other necessary stuff is obviously expensive,
so I would not recommend choosing this engine 
if you don’t have the extra money to fix this.
I mean you can buy it, but I would rather a buy a cement mixer or something.
-Next there is the GTI version equipped with a 2.0 l TSI engine which can have a couple of problems as well.
In this case again the damn timing chain mechanism can be a bit problematic,
specifically the very first weaker version of the timing chain tensioner can fail,
and damage your engine even before 100 000 km.
since there is a noticeable difference between the old and the updated tensioner.
-the next problematic part of this engine is called the camshaft bridge
which can occasionally cause oil starvation in the cylinder head or other damage if this small screen falls out from it.
The good thing is that only the cars made to 2009 are more prone to this,
since they have the earliest version of the camshaft bridge.
But the bad things is,
that the cam bridge was revised more than 3 times so the screen can fall out on later cars as well.
After this, there is the plastic variable intake manifold 
which can be faulty.
This is a complex plastic garbage with moving plastic flaps in it which can wear out and fail and shit
+ it can also cause  vacuum leaks, so be prepared to replace it with a newer, better and more sturdy updated manifold.
Next there is the PCV valve which can be often faulty before 80 000 mi.
It’s good to replace it preventively since it can blow the rear main seal which starts to leak oil
and that’s an expensive repair.
-before I move onto the most powerful versions, I have to mention the infamous 1.8 l TSI which was interestingly also available in this Golf even though it’s not very common.
This is the same engine which was available in the Audi A4 B8,
and it also has the same common problems as the already mentioned 2.0 l GTI engine.
But except all these issues it also has a very high chance of excessive oil consumption because of the undersized pistons,
piston rings and oil scraper rings.
-lastly there is the Golf GTI edition 35 and the Golf  R both equipped with an older generation 2.0 l TSI engine.
This unit has indeed an older construction but it’s also more reliable than the engine in the regular GTI.
It’s mainly because it has a timing belt instead of a timing chain and it also has a slightly different - better intake manifold.
From the weak points of this engine, the only thing worth mentioning is the HPFP camshaft follower
which you should check / eventually replace since it can get worn and cause issues in the future.
To finally end this journey of engine hell,
I have to mention that all of the direct injection petrol engines can have often issues with leaking water pump so check the coolant level regularly
+ let’s not forget about the other possible issues of these fantastic engines like the:
carbon build up, faulty injectors, faulty ignition coils or  occasionally bigger or smaller oil consumption.
All of the diesel engines can easily reach 300 000 km or 400 000 km,
but of course they can have the regular diesel engine problems which can occur much earlier.
-So the EGR valve can be faulty which is not like the end of the world, but replacing it is not that easy and not that cheap since it’s mounted on the back of the engine
-then the injectors can be faulty usually just after 200  000 km, but occasionally even before 200 000 km or at around this mileage more often on the 1.6 l TDI
-next, the bosch CP4 high pressure fuel pump can fail and in this case it will release
tiny metal particles in the whole fuel system which will destroy the injectors too.
This issue can occur for the most part only in the US or in some parts of Eastern EU,
because of the different quality of the fuel, but even here it’s not like extremely common and if you will practice
these things then you can minimize the possibility of this issue.
-after this it’s good to mention the infamous emission 
scandal and the associated software update
which should correct the emissions, because 
some owners experienced these strange issues
after this update. But the good thing is that because of this emission scandal,
there still should be an extended warranty in the US for 
all the main parts of the diesel engines.
Lastly if you are buying one of the more powerful 
2.0 l TDI engine made to 2009 which has this,
or this engine code then at approx. 200 000 km it’s a good idea
to remove the oil pan and check the oil pump drive shaft which can be worn out and later cause loss of oil pressure which is not good.
All the petrol engines are equipped with a timing chain except the older 1.4 l and the 1.6 l naturally aspirated engines which have a timing belt.
As I already said,
the chain mechanism in the 4 cylinder engines can be worn anytime basically, so even before 100 000 km.
That’s why the best is to either measure how much is it worn or to replace it preventively after buying mainly in the early engines made to mid 2011.
Because keep in mind that if the chain skips then it can easily damage the engine pretty badly.
This VW can be equipped with the 5  or 6 speed manual gearbox or there are three types of automatic transmissions.
-The manual transmissions are usually reliable 
just check them for strange noises and it’s good
to occasionally replace the oil in them. The Dual 
mass flywheel can be of course worn
if the car is equipped with it, but it usually wears out just around 200 000 km, even though
this mostly depends on how the previous owner used the car.
-From the automatic transmissions the regular 6 speed Tiptronic is the most reliable, but sadly this gearbox was mated only to the 2.5 l 5 cylinder petrol engine
-On the other side, the 6 and 7 speed DSG dual clutch gearboxes are not that reliable.
Especially the 7 speed version can have often issues with the mechatronic
and also the clutches can wear out even before 
100 000 km.
+ the DSG gearbox also has a dual mass flywheel which can be worn so keep extra money for the DSG issues
and for more information about these transmissions check out my website!
If you are buying a model equipped with the 4motion 4wd system then make sure that the 4wd is working properly
–so check for front wheel spin since the haldex pump can fail and if it fails then the car is going to be just front wheel drive.
Because of this it’s really important to change the oil in the differential every 50 000 or max 60 000 km
and also change the filter in it which can clog and cause premature failure of the already mentioned haldex pump.
To summarize things up: -the older naturally aspirated petrol engines are the most reliable
-avoid the DSG gearbox unless you have additional 2 000 € to fix it
-avoid cars with performance upgrades and with questionable 
maintenance history
+ keep at least 1000 € for the maintenance and possible repairs, but if you are buying a car with a direct injection petrol engine
or with a diesel engine then keep at least 2000 €, 
and to top of that if you want the more powerful
1.4 tsi twincharger or the GTI model then keep at 
least 3 000€
And as always if you have personal  experience with this car or more information about it, then you can write it into comments!

To summarize things up: -the older naturally aspirated petrol engines are the most reliable
-avoid the DSG gearbox unless you have additional 2 000 € to fix it

-avoid cars with performance upgrades and with questionable 
maintenance history
+ keep at least 1000 € for the maintenance and possible repairs, but if you are buying a car with a direct injection petrol engine

or with a diesel engine then keep at least 2000 €, 
and to top of that if you want the more powerful

1.4 tsi twincharger or the GTI model then keep at 
least 3 000€
And as always if you have personal  experience with this car or more information about it, then you can write it into comments!

videos.title: Volkswagen’s 1.5 TSI engine: Common problems and advantages
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.5 TSI engine belongs to the EA211 
family, and it was first introduced in
2014. The company has been using these 
engines in almost all kinds of models,
starting with the Polo and up to the Passat, 
Touran, or even Arteon. Also, Audi, Seat,
and Skoda models have been using this engine 
heavily, and now it’s one of the most widespread
modern-generation engines in Volkswagen’s lineup.
Even though the TSI type of engines got a lot of
hatred when they first appeared about 20 years 
ago, now they are considered quite reliable,
very economical, efficient, and basically 
non-problematic engines. The 1.5 TSI is also
available as the mild-hybrid engine, 1.5 eTSI, 
and it utilizes the same base, so everything in
this video will cover that hybrid version, too.
Please keep in mind that I will focus on common
problems, so the video may seem a little 
negative. But I personally think that the
1.5 TSI engine is quite good and only has several 
drawbacks that owners just need to know about.
First of all, starting from the very beginning 
of its life and up to model year 2024,
these engines had a very disturbing feature known 
as the kangaroo effect. It appeared to torture
owners of cars with manual transmissions. Once 
you start driving in the first gear, the engine
may suddenly lower RPMs and nearly stall, but then 
everything comes back to normal. It seems like you
are a bad driver, and it may be quite embarrassing 
at times. Fortunately, the most recent updates
seem to have finally fixed this issue. But 
if you still experience it, try releasing
the clutch pedal completely before you start 
pressing the gas pedal. This should help a lot.
The compression ratio of 12.5 to 1 is not typical 
for petrol engines, so I believe using low-octane
fuel is not an option. European classification 
octane number 95 or higher is recommended by
the manufacturer, but owners admit that 98 
petrol works well, while anything lower than
that may cause slight knocking and loss of power.
Also, these engines are able to deactivate two of
the cylinders, shifting one of the camshafts to 
another position. The system looks quite good,
but experts still don’t know if it’s 
going to last long enough. For now,
there haven’t been any serious problems 
with this cylinder deactivation system, so I
believe it’s never going to be a serious problem.
The engine uses a variable geometry turbocharger,
which is also not that typical for petrol 
engines. And I know about some cases when
these turbos failed and required replacement, 
but I wouldn’t say the problem is very common.
The engine is equipped with the timing belt, and 
the service requirements are very tangled. In the
first generation of the 1.5 TSI engine, Volkswagen 
recommended cambelt replacement once every 5 years
or 140,000 miles or 225,000 kilometers. After 
updates in 2023, the engine has two types of
recommendations: no requirements for belt 
replacement or changing once every 15 years
or 180,000 miles, 300,000 kilometers. Basically, 
the belt is considered for the entire lifespan
of the engine, but I would replace it at 150K 
miles anyway if I wanted to drive this car for
long enough. This is a simple dry belt system, 
but it’s not very cheap to replace, and there
is no evidence that the belt is problematic, 
so no need to replace it once every 5 years.
Other than that, there is a common issue of oil 
consumption after the engine hits 100,000 miles
or 150,000 kilometers. So, high-mileage engines 
will need to be checked for oil level regularly.
I can tell you that even though I’m not 
that into Volkswagen cars and technologies,
this 1.5 TSI engine seems to be a great machine. 
The company learned its lessons with the early
1.4 TSI mistakes and made a significantly 
better engine. I hope this video was helpful,
and I also hope that you will write in the 
comments about your experience with these engines.

videos.title: Renault Espace V 1.6 dCi (2016) - POV Drive
Double Clutch Repair - Renault DC4|Smart H-DTC|Hyundai & Kia D6GF1|Ford 1.0 DPS6 - LuK RepSet 2CT
videos.transcript_text:
Removing/Installing the Double Clutch
Ford 1.0-litre, DPS6 6-speed transmission
Hyundai, Kia, D6GF1 6-speed transmission
Renault, Dacia, DC0/DC4 6-speed transmission
Smart, H-DCT 6-speed transmission
Mercedes Benz, 6G-DCT  6-speed transmission
Geely, 6DCT 6-speed transmission
using a Renault (diesel engine) with DC4 transmission as an example
In conjunction with a LuK RepSet 2CT and the LuK special tool.
Attention!
Due to on-going technical developments in production by the vehicle manufacturer, the repair process and the special tools are subject to change.
This video shows an example of the necessary procedures and is intended to supplement the current LuK technical brochures. Repair work should only be carried out by personnel with the necessary specialised qualifications at suitable workshops using the latest repair instructions and corresponding special tools.
The latest data and information can be found at: www.repxpert.com
Remove the transmission, observing the vehicle manufacturer's instructions.
During removal of the transmission, insert the plugs into the openings in the differential.
Position the support sleeve (KL-0500-8214) on the hollow shaft.
Hyundai, Kia:
– Use support sleeve (KL-0500-8212A)
Renault, Dacia (petrol engine), Ford, Smart, Mercedes Benz, Geely:
– Use support sleeve (KL-0500-8214) with spacer (KL-0500-8215)
Renault (diesel engine):
Guide the detent pin (KL-0500-8210A) over the sleeve.
The markings "1" must face the hooks.
Renault, Dacia (petrol engine), Hyundai, Kia, Ford, Smart, Mercedes Benz, Geely:
The markings "2" must face the hooks.
Remove both actuators.
Check that the adapter sleeves and dowel pins are securely in place.
Clean the transmission input shafts.
Check both radial shaft seals for leaks.
Check the condition of the bearing seat on the hollow shaft.
Use new screws. Apply a tightening torque of 8 Nm.
Hyundai, Kia: Apply a tightening torque of 5 Nm.
First, insert the lever actuator for clutch K2 (narrow fork opening).
When inserting both lever actuators, ensure that the adapter sleeves and dowel pins are positioned correctly.
Insert both actuators.
Use new screws. Apply a tightening torque of 19 Nm.
Remove both transport fasteners.
The last four digits on the lever actuator and the middle four digits on the return spring must be identical.
Tighten all return springs. Apply a tightening torque of 26 Nm.
Align the return springs. The markings must face each other.
Lubricate the gearing on the transmission input shafts with a suitable lubricant (in line with the instructions from the vehicle manufacturer; alternatively use Castrol Olista Longtime 2 or 3, for example).
Moisten the bearing seat on the hollow shaft with a drop of transmission fluid.
To insert the new double clutch, position the tool as if it were being used for removal.
Position the pressure sleeve (KL-0500-8213).
Hyundai, Kia:
– Use pressure sleeve (KL-0500-8211A)
Renault, Dacia (gasoline engine), Ford, Smart, Mercedes Benz, Geely:
– Use pressure sleeve (KL-0500-8213) with spacer (KL-0500-8215)"
Observe the maximum permissible clearance of 7 mm. If the clearance is greater, the clutch disc will not engage with the gearing of the hollow shaft.
Secure the threaded pins on the transmission housing.
Hyundai, Kia: Use threaded pins with a fine thread (KL-0500-8216) from
the tool box (part no. 400 0470 10).
Set the torque wrench to 9 Nm.
The press-fitting process is complete when:
– The circlip groove is fully visible
– The force required to rotate the threaded spindle increases significantly
The force applied to the threaded spindle must not result in the torque wrench being released. If the torque wrench is released before the clutch has reached its end position, the installation has not been completed correctly."
Mount the snap ring with the narrow section of the opening facing upwards.
Insert the snap ring so that the gap sits either side of the large tooth.
Release both transport fasteners from the double clutch.
To do this, rotate the release key in an anti-clockwise direction until a clicking sound is heard (maximum of 12 revolutions)."
Important: The release key is preloaded.
Release it gently!
Coat the internal gearing of the lever actuators and actuator shafts with an extremely thin layer of grease.
If the gearing fails to engage, rotate the actuator's toothed gear.
Use new screws. Apply a tightening torque of 5.5 Nm.
Install the transmission in accordance with the vehicle manufacturer's instructions and check the gear oil level, topping up as necessary.
Use the appropriate diagnostic tool to complete the basic adjustment of the clutch system.

Renault, Dacia (petrol engine), Hyundai, Kia, Ford, Smart, Mercedes Benz, Geely:
The markings "2" must face the hooks.
Remove both actuators.
Check that the adapter sleeves and dowel pins are securely in place.
Clean the transmission input shafts.
Check both radial shaft seals for leaks.
Check the condition of the bearing seat on the hollow shaft.

Use new screws. Apply a tightening torque of 8 Nm.
Hyundai, Kia: Apply a tightening torque of 5 Nm.
First, insert the lever actuator for clutch K2 (narrow fork opening).
When inserting both lever actuators, ensure that the adapter sleeves and dowel pins are positioned correctly.
Insert both actuators.
Use new screws. Apply a tightening torque of 19 Nm.
Remove both transport fasteners.
The last four digits on the lever actuator and the middle four digits on the return spring must be identical.
Tighten all return springs. Apply a tightening torque of 26 Nm.
Align the return springs. The markings must face each other.

Lubricate the gearing on the transmission input shafts with a suitable lubricant (in line with the instructions from the vehicle manufacturer; alternatively use Castrol Olista Longtime 2 or 3, for example).
Moisten the bearing seat on the hollow shaft with a drop of transmission fluid.
To insert the new double clutch, position the tool as if it were being used for removal.

Position the pressure sleeve (KL-0500-8213).
Hyundai, Kia:
– Use pressure sleeve (KL-0500-8211A)
Renault, Dacia (gasoline engine), Ford, Smart, Mercedes Benz, Geely:
– Use pressure sleeve (KL-0500-8213) with spacer (KL-0500-8215)"
Observe the maximum permissible clearance of 7 mm. If the clearance is greater, the clutch disc will not engage with the gearing of the hollow shaft.

Secure the threaded pins on the transmission housing.
Hyundai, Kia: Use threaded pins with a fine thread (KL-0500-8216) from
the tool box (part no. 400 0470 10).
Set the torque wrench to 9 Nm.

The press-fitting process is complete when:
– The circlip groove is fully visible
– The force required to rotate the threaded spindle increases significantly
The force applied to the threaded spindle must not result in the torque wrench being released. If the torque wrench is released before the clutch has reached its end position, the installation has not been completed correctly."
Mount the snap ring with the narrow section of the opening facing upwards.
Insert the snap ring so that the gap sits either side of the large tooth.

Release both transport fasteners from the double clutch.
To do this, rotate the release key in an anti-clockwise direction until a clicking sound is heard (maximum of 12 revolutions)."

Important: The release key is preloaded.
Release it gently!
Coat the internal gearing of the lever actuators and actuator shafts with an extremely thin layer of grease.
If the gearing fails to engage, rotate the actuator's toothed gear.
Use new screws. Apply a tightening torque of 5.5 Nm.
Install the transmission in accordance with the vehicle manufacturer's instructions and check the gear oil level, topping up as necessary.
Use the appropriate diagnostic tool to complete the basic adjustment of the clutch system.

“Engine Fault, Repair Needed” in Vauxhall, Opel, Peugeot, Citroen, etc. What’s this?
videos.transcript_text:
To cut a long story short, the “Engine Fault, 
Repair Needed!” error message is something like
the check engine light in your car. In a lot 
of cases, you will be able to spot the reason
for this message by looking into the emission 
system, engine sensors, or AdBlue system. But
there is one thing you should check first.
And this is the battery. About half of all
cases when people come to the dealership with 
the Engine Fault Repair Needed message are about
dying 12V batteries. In most cars, they are AGM 
and once they start malfunctioning, they need to
be replaced. You may also try to charge such 
a battery with an appropriate battery tender.
Especially if it’s younger than 3 years old.
It’s very common to see this message as a ghost.
You see it right when you start the engine, then 
you may also see other lights and warnings like
the EPS lights, Brake System warning lights, and 
some random error messages. But once you restart
the vehicle, these issues disappear and your car 
may continue working normally. Just check the
battery in this case prior to paying your money 
for dozens of inspections in the dealership!
Also, this message may be triggered by the issues 
with fuel combustion. If your engine misfires due
to bad plugs or a certain sensor is faulty, you 
may see the Engine Fault Repair Needed message.
But in these cases, it’s easy to diagnose the 
problem. Once you hook up a good scanner tool,
you will obviously see the actual problem.
Also, AdBlue-related issues are very common
for this message. In some cases, the 
AdBlue pump will need replacement. But
don’t invest in this before you are sure 
this is the reason for the error message.
I’ve written several articles about this 
message in my blog, so I will give you the
links in the description for further research.
Now a couple of words about the cars that are
prone to this message. These are primarily 
Peugeot and Citroen vehicles in Europe with
various diesel engines. Also, Vauxhall and Opel 
cars that started using Peugeot engines recently
may throw this message. What surprised me a lot 
is that the Toyota Proace can throw the Engine
Fault Repair Needed message and when I researched 
a little more, I found out that the Proace uses
Peugeot engines in Europe and is basically 
the twin of Peugeot-Citroen vans like the
Traveller or the Jumpy. Apparently, they share the 
software and hence have the same error messages.
So, whatever vehicle you have, if you 
see the Engine Fault Repair Needed,
start with the battery. And then go on to check 
the AdBlue system, engine sensors, and misfiring.

starts to glow and in cold temperatures
you may struggle to get enough heat to
start that ignition process in the
engine itself so the glow plug actually
raises the cylinder temperatures so the
intake air and fuel are at a high enough
temperature to combust when the
compression is at the correct point so
most garages will actually replace the
glow plugs as soon as they hear about
cold start issues because it is quite a
common thing but actually you should
check your glow plugs you can test if
they're working or not if you just put a
voltmeter between them and the power
supply and just check they are getting
in enough voltage so if your engine
always struggles on very cold mornings
but on warmer days it's not struggling
to start and you have no trouble at all
starting the engine when it's warm it
could well be the glow plugs so get them
tested and checked and if there's a sign

or they're not doing their job properly
replace them it's a relatively cheap fix

other systems within the engine so if
there is a problem with the voltage it's
going to affect so many different areas
of the car and on a cold day the battery
voltage will generally drop so you might
have a battery that's working perfectly

that temperature starts to drop the
battery efficiency will degrade and that
working battery that was only just
working is now going to fail on you in

expose the weakness in the battery

will typically manifest itself in Long
start problems and if your battery is

a good idea to dip the clutch on most
diesel engines when you actually start

starter motor is only turning the engine
so a simple checklist rear really that
we should put up just to diagnose cold
start problems the first one is to check
that the battery is properly connected
and it's in a good state so bad Earth
connections can cause all sorts of
intermittent faults with the car it's
not generally limited to starting issues
so if you're getting other problems in
the electrical system of the car it
could well be the battery or the
connections to and from the battery or a
short somewhere in the system so in some
cold climates people actually use
battery warmers it's interesting that at
zero degrees Fahrenheit a battery can

degrees Fahrenheit it can lose about 35
percent of its power so just warming
that battery up will certainly help to
improve its efficiency and may just lift
you over that threshold of not being
able to start your diesel engine so
that's for people that live in really
really cold climates and we've had some
really extreme cold weather lately so
that may apply to you this year whereas
in previous years you've not been
worried about it so check the glow plugs
are functioning prop quickly check the
voltage they should be getting 12 volts
when they kick in if they're not getting
the full 12 volts or there's some sort
of problem with the circuit there you
need to address that and just make sure
that's fixed because those glow plugs
are really vital on cold days I always
recommend to people to actually wait for
the glow plug light to go out when they
start the engine just to get into a
habit on most modern diesels and in most
environments you can get away with just
starting the engine but it's just good
practice to get into just to check your
dashboard lights as you turn the
ignition key and just make sure
everything settles before you actually
turn the starter so we've spoken about
the cranking ability of the engine so if
you've got the wrong grade of oil it
will not reduce the friction to the
point where the engine can effectively
start itself so you may need to switch

the systems in the car and just see if
