again helped to isolate the problem to
that isolation circuit that helps to
prevent the voltage draining when you
actually start the car and need all the
power in the starter so fuel additives

videos.transcript_text:
I have owned and carried the Ruger RXM
since I purchased it back in February
and it's probably my favorite gun in
2025. And in this video, I want to give
you my honest thoughts about the Ruger
RXM, what I do, what I don't like about
it, especially after having carried it
almost every single day, and how I think
it performs out on the range.
Now, I purchased the Ruger RXM to go
alongside my everyday carry with the
Hellcat Pro. I wanted something that was
just slightly larger and could flex into
that space of home defense, concealed
carry, and just something I enjoyed
shooting out on the range. More
specifically, I was attracted to the
fact that I feel like Ruger and Magpul
fixed all of the things that I just
didn't like about the original Glock 19.
Plus with the fire control insert, it
means that you get a world of
possibilities, especially as time goes
on and companies catch up. Means you're
going to have the option for a barrel,
slide, frame combination such as the
G26, the 43X, 17, the list goes on and
on. And since I just started this
channel, I would love to make more
reviews for you all. This video will
probably never be monetized. Please
subscribe, give it a thumbs up, anything
to help the algorithm goes a long way. I
also love the fact that Magpul adjusted
the Glock grip angle, so it's no longer
that 22° cant, it's more along the lines
of your traditional 1911. In this case,
it means that I don't have to cant my
wrist more than I typically do with all
of my other firearms when I shoot the
RXM. Which I think this alone makes it
really attractive for people who want
the reliability and the customization of
Glock, but don't want to have to switch
their technique on a different platform.
And another big benefit of the RXM is
going to be the compatibility with Glock
Gen 3 parts. And in my opinion, because
Glock really hasn't innovated much, they
don't typically stray outside of their
core platforms, it's created this market
where there is a ton of aftermarket
upgrades and optionality, whether it be
you want to update the trigger, the
barrel, the slide, if you want to mill
it, if you want to put an optic, if you
want a magwell, you kind of get my
point. In this case, I've not done any
updates to my RXM except swap out the
frame from the original gray to the OD
green just because it matched the Magpul
furniture of my AR and I thought it
looked really cool. And then added the
Holosun 407K on it and the Streamlight
TLR-7X. Eventually, I do want to swap
out the barrel to the Aim Surplus Just
the Tip barrel. However, for now, it
shoots great and I really like it. And
if you are familiar with Glock style
triggers, the RXM has a Glock style
trigger. Maybe marginally better than
the Gen 3, but it's a little worse than
the Gen 5 Glocks. And in this case,
you're still going to get that rolling
break, it's going to be pretty spongy,
and it just is what it is. But honestly,
after shooting it for a while and
especially compared to the Hellcat Pro,
it's got a good enough trigger. I'll
finish this section by saying there are
a lot of other things I like about the
RXM. In this case, I really like the
integrated magwell. I love the universal
mounting pattern that they did with the
optics plate system and I think the grip
texture is really solid. It's It gives
you a really solid purchase on the
firearm, but it's not overly aggressive,
especially when I am carrying all day.
At this point, I put roughly around 750
rounds through the RXM and I really like
the way it shoots. I've actually really
bonded with this gun in a way I wasn't
super expecting. First and foremost, I
think just because of the size of this
platform and just the magwell, it really
helps push my hand back up into the
trigger well and the extended beaver
tail really just helps me get a really
confident grip on the firearm where I
feel like I can handle the recoil and
manage it really, really well. And I do
find that the Ruger RXM is super fun and
easy to shoot. I think it's just big
enough to conceal and hide well enough
underneath clothing, but it's also big
enough for me to feel comfortable
getting a strong grip on the platform
and being able to shoot it confidently.
This is also where I really appreciate
the more traditional grip angle of the
RXM over a Glock. In this case, I don't
have to get used to a different cant on
my wrist and readjust the way I acquire
my sights when I switch from platform to
platform. In this case, the RXM feels
like every other polymer striker fired
pistol that I own and I like that
because it means when I go to the range
or in a self-defense situation, I know
right where I need to go and that muscle
memory is already ingrained. Now, to
move along to some of the negatives of
this firearm, I will say initially when
I purchased it, I did notice with the
original barrel that it had some tooling
or kind of barrel marks inside of it. In
this case, I reached out to Ruger and
with pretty much no questions asked,
they just sent me a new one. So, kudos
to Ruger there. The other con that I
will say is I do notice a bit of a
tolerance issue with the way the slide
interacts with the Magpul frames. In
this case, I do find that there's this
little bit of a gap, no matter if I use
the original gray frame I have or the
updated gray frame that Ruger sent me
when I complained about it or the
aftermarket OD green one that I
purchased from Magpul, all of them kind
of have the same gap where the front of
the barrel and the slide are going to be
a little bit separated from the actual
frame, more so than I've seen in any
other polymer type handgun. Hopefully,
as time goes on, Ruger figures out how
to tighten up their tolerances and the
quality control there. But past that,
I've not had a single malfunction, I've
not had any issues with the firearm past
that and it shot just awesome. Now,
unfortunately, I'm probably not the best
sample size because when I go to the
range, I typically just buy 115, 124
grain brass from Blazer. And in this
case, because it's already pretty good
ammo, I've not really had any issues and
I'm not really trying to buy cheap ammo
to induce a malfunction because I'm
there to just have fun and shoot and
enjoy what I'm doing. Lastly, I will say
there is an initial break-in period of
around 300 lbs. I also did do an
internal polish of some of the parts and
just that 25 cent Glock kind of trigger
job that you see online. And that did
help kind of crisp things up a little
bit, but just know that if you decide to
purchase this firearm, give it a couple
hundred rounds and that trigger will
start to smooth out more and more.
Now, as far as concealing the RXM, this
is definitely going to be different for
each person. In this case, I am 6'1, I
weigh around 185 lbs, and I've got more
of a tall kind of ectomorphic style
build. Which just means larger handguns
are going to be harder for me to
conceal. In this case, I would say the
RXM is super easy for me to conceal in
normal fall, winter clothes. And quite
frankly, almost anyone can carry a giant
gun whenever you've got tons of layers
to hide the firearm. The real challenge
really just comes down to summer and
warmer months. And in this case, when
you're wearing shorts and a t-shirt and
being able to hide that confidently. In
this case, I do have a sidecar appendix
holster for my RXM, which does allow me
to conceal the RXM, my TLR-7X, and an
extra 15 round magazine. This is
definitely a bulky setup to begin with
and eventually, I plan to buy just a
dedicated holster for the RXM, slim up
things a little bit more. However, I can
say I do feel like I conceal the RXM
well even with a relatively
tight-fitting shirt. In this case,
having a concealment claw on the holster
definitely helps. And then also just
wearing darker colors. And let's be
honest, most people, almost everyone,
will never, ever notice if you are
printing. They're too busy looking at
their phones. Now, if I do find that the
outfit that I'm wearing, it just doesn't
work, I'll typically switch to the
Hellcat Pro. And I also just bought the
Canik Mete MC9 for something even
smaller as well. Now, pivoting to home
defense, I think the RXM is a
spectacular option. In this case, it's
why I mounted the TLR-7X on my handgun.
And I know right off the bat, that is
going to be polarizing because some
people think you shouldn't have a weapon
mounted light, some people do. In this
case, I always carry a flashlight on me
every single day, which would be my
first line of instinct is to grab that
if I ever need. And then in a
self-defense situation, I have it on my
firearm if I need it. And I do keep my
firearms locked up because I've got
young kids at home.
So, is the Ruger RXM worth buying? In my
opinion, absolutely. I think it's close
to one of the best bang for buck options
out there on the market right now. And
in this case, you can typically find the
RXM for roughly 375 bucks, sometimes
less, sometimes a little more. Ruger
also just added a threaded barrel
option, so if you want to add a
suppressor or compensator, you can for
just a little bit more. I also do think
the modularity of the platform creates a
ton of value for people. And as
companies start to offer more slides,
and barrels, and frame combinations,
you're going to be able to have even
more options, create a PCC, a PDW, all
while having the same one serialized
part. I also just think having
aftermarket availability and the access
to a ton of additional parts for the
RXM, it's going to mean that no matter
who you are, you can find what you want,
whether it's upgrading the trigger or
the sights, etc. And lastly, I think the
RXM is the perfect Glock for people who
don't like Glock. The RXM offers a ton
of upgrades over the original Glock 19
Gen 3 and even the Gen 5 right out of
the box. And because of the improvements
with the grip angle, I think more people
will be willing to step into the RXM
than have to learn a new technique and
adjust the way they cant their wrist
with what Glock has to offer. So, with
all that said, what are your thoughts?
Did you buy the RXM? And if not, what
have you bought instead? And if you are
curious on what an $800 handgun gets
you, watch this next video on the
Walther PDP Pro. I'll see you guys next
time.
Bye.

videos.title: GM 2.0L Ecotec LTG Engine - Overview, Problems & Reliability
videos.transcript_text:
The 2.0 Ecotec LTG is a turbocharged 2-liter
inline four-cylinder engine featuring direct
fuel injection.
It is a member of General Motors' Gen3 Ecotec
engine family.These days, GM incorporates
it into a variety of cars, such as the 2.0L
Turbo Chevrolet Camaro.
Let's examine the 2.0 Ecotec LTG engine's
construction, typical issues, and dependability
in more detail. It’s the Car Problems Youtube
channel. Subscribe and let’s get started!
Engine Overview
The 2.0 Ecotec LTG engine is entirely new
and has no connection to the 2.0L LHU engine
that is currently in use. The LTG engine uses
a new open-deck style sand-cast aluminum cylinder
block with cast-in-place iron liners and enhanced
structural support, even though the blocks
are dimensionally similar. To handle higher
engine loads, the cylinder bore walls and
main bearing bulkheads have been reinforced.
Lightweight cast aluminum pistons with a dish-shaped
piston crown, forged powdered metal connecting
rods, and a crankshaft made of steel comprise
the rotating assembly.
An oil pump with two stages and variable displacement
powers the oiling system. The variable-flow
oiling system prevents energy wastage from
pumping unnecessary oil, maximizing fuel efficiency.
A heat exchanger that is linked to the engine's
coolant circuit cools engine oil. An oil pan-installed
modular balancing shaft system assures smooth
engine operation.
The 16-valve aluminum cylinder head of the
LTG 2.0 Turbo engine is built for high boost
pressure and direct fuel injection. Stainless
steel intake valves and sodium-filled exhaust
valves are installed on the cylinder head.
Additionally, the engine has a DOHC design
with CVVT, or continuously variable valve
timing. A timing chain drives the camshafts
on the intake and exhaust. Low-friction hydraulic
roller-finger followers are used to actuate
valves.
Extended-life spark plugs, capable of lasting
up to 100,000 miles (160,000 km), are used
with LTG heads. There are two fuel pumps in
the fuel system. The first is a standard gasoline
pump in the fuel tank that is powered by electricity.
Fuel is sent to the second pump, which is
a high-pressure fuel pump mounted on the engine
and powered by the intake camshaft. Fuel pressure
is supplied by the HP pump between 750 and
2,250 psi. A pressure-regulated fuel rail
and a high-pressure stainless steel feed line
deliver fuel to the injectors.
A BorgWarner twin-scroll turbocharger with
an electronically controlled wastegate powers
the 2.0L LTG Ecotec. The maximum boost produced
by the turbo is about 20 psi.
The intake manifold has a plastic construction.
The brake booster has no source of vacuum
because the intake system is pressurized.
The engine in this instance has a vacuum pump
driven by a cam that is positioned behind
the cylinder head. The exhaust camshaft powers
it.
Problems and Reliability
Let's start with the fact that 2.0 Ecotec
LTG is a good engine. It boasts the performance
of 3.0 or even 4.0-liter naturally aspirated
V6 and V8, along with a small four-cylinder
engine's excellent fuel efficiency. It's the
first inline-4 engine in a Camaro since the
gen-3 model, by the way. However is the 2.0
LTG Ecotec dependable despite being the industry's
most powerful car engine? This turbo-four
offers a good balance between performance
and reliability, which is surprising. It is
not flawless, of course, just like everything
else in the world.
Carbon Build-up
Every direct-injected engine experiences carbon
buildup on the intake valves to some degree.
Nor is the well-known drawback of direct injection
exclusive to the 2.0 LTG Ecotec. Some oil
may be blown into the intake by all engines.
It is not an issue for those using conventional
port injection since fuel washes everything
back into the combustion chambers.
However, blow-by oil deposits on the intake
valves and surrounding surfaces occur with
direct injection, where gasoline is injected
straight into the combustion chamber, obstructing
the intake valves and ports. The amount of
airflow restriction caused by this unclean,
black buildup may be such that it compromises
dependability and performance. This typically
occurs every 80000 to 100000 miles. One useful
technique for reviving some dead horses is
walnut blasting.
Timing Cover Oil Leak
Another prevalent issue with LTG engines is
oil leaks around the timing cover. Typically,
there are slow-seeping oil leaks that burn
off on the engine block, giving off some smells
of burning oil along with little smoke. Look
for black spots on the cylinder block surrounding
the timing cover if you experience any of
these symptoms. There could be a timing cover
oil leak.
Piston Failures
Some 2.0 Turbo Ecotec vehicles had piston
failures within the first few thousand miles
of sales in the early years. These early motor
flaws were swiftly fixed by GM, and it appears
that these problems are no longer present
in later models. On the 2.0 LTG, the pistons
are not the strongest component of the engine,
though. They don't have a lot of safety margin
because they are cast aluminum rather than
forged. They function perfectly on a stock
engine. If you want to increase the power
output, it is recommended to replace the factory
pistons with aftermarket forged aluminum ones.
Summary
Remember that the 2.0-liter Ecotec LTG turbocharged
engine is a high-performance heart of the
vehicle. There is no denying that it requires
more maintenance. Premium gasoline, high-grade
synthetic oils, and pricey spark plugs are
needed for the engine. In addition, due to
its intricate design, there is a great deal
of potential for unforeseen problems with
the electronics, turbo, and emissions apparatus.
The 2.0 Ecotec LTG engine itself ought to
last for well over 200000 miles if it is maintained
properly.
